utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness have, please, in the B/C/S text, and I'd like to forecast that the Chamber may have brought their own copies with them. But if the usher could display on the overhead projector from the English text. If the usher could display from the English text first page 57, which is page 42 in the B/C/S for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this is a passage dealing with the memorandum we've discussed with earlier witnesses, but Ms. Budding's report, at the top of the page, is as follows in a conclusion --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we are getting English translations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Start again, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to find the passage Mr. Nice indicated in the English version, but page 57 simply doesn't exist, and he refers to 57. The last page in the text I have is 53 of the English text. Audrey Budding, that report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, it goes beyond that. Would the usher please check to ensure that Mr. Milosevic has the right text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other pages that I have begin with page 1 and go on to 29, page 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He's looking at the B/C/S version, I understand. He can have an English version if we've got a spare, but it's going on the overhead projector, and can the accused please look at page 42, which is in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the expert conclusion, as we can see, is in part to this effect: "My own opinion is that the Memorandum is most important as an indicator: As evidence that by 1986 the assertions it set out were accepted by influential figures within Serbia's intellectual elite. To put it as clearly as possible, it was the existence of the belief system set out in the Memorandum, far more than the Memorandum itself, that influenced the process of Yugoslavia's dissolution." Now, Mr. Terzic, it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice. Mr. Terzic, is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there's a problem here. I do have page 42, but I can't find that passage. Could you assist me, please. Where does that passage begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In a paragraph beginning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not having B/C/S, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've marked the beginning of the paragraph. Yes. That's it there. Now, my only question --

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that's not what Mr. Nice is reading. Ah, yes, I found it. I found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I seek your assistance to track the important landmarks of the belief system. Do you follow what I'm doing? She says there's a belief system reflected in the memorandum, and it's that belief system that I want to track. All right? And with that in mind, can we then come back to page 5 in the English and page 4 in the B/C/S. And I'm going to deal with certain entries in her report sequentially, not necessarily absolutely chronologically. On the screen we can see this passage: "Into this situation of growing conflict came the first of Kosovo's twentieth-century episodes of status-reversal: Its passage from Ottoman to Serbian rule in the Balkan Wars." And then this sentence: "Contemporary observers of the Balkan wars noted numerous atrocities committed by Serbian and Montenegrin soldiers. Some saw evidence that the Serbian soldiers were engaged in a systematic attempt to alter the demographic balance of the region in order to justify its incorporation into the Serbian state." Do you have any challenge to what Audrey Budding writes there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, for my part I am keeping my finger in the end notes to see the authorities that Audrey Budding refers to, and this is at page 74.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're asking him to comment on both passages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, on the passage we've just looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What about the passage on page 57?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. 57 was an introduction. I'm exploring the belief system through various parts of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Serbian soldiers engaged in a systematic attempt to alter the demographic balance." Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice has asked two questions. I don't know what order to take them in. Shall I start from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, has put one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question I'm dealing with is the question on your page 4 which is: Were the Serbian soldiers engaged in a systematic attempt to alter the demographic balance? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I assume you'll agree that I cannot give a yes or no question to such a complicated question. However, if I might be allowed to state something briefly, then I can say no, and I can explain that by backing it up with a few sentences, with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not challenging, I'm not disputing the fact that, like in any other war conflict, and this was a conflict not between the Serbs and the Albanians, this was the first Balkan war, a conflict between the Balkan Christian states, that is to say Serbia, Montenegro, Bulgaria, and Greece on the one hand against the Ottoman Empire on the other. And this position taken by Ms. Budding is based on the Carnegie Foundation Institute report dating back to 1914. However, many more sources from the ground, from the terrain, have registered and recorded incidents that occur in every war, and I'm not challenging that. However, there was no plan on the part of the Serbian government to ethnically cleanse that territory, because had such a plan existed, had there been such a plan, it could have been implemented, it would have been implemented. And as proof of that I offer Adolf Fischer's book, a Swiss physician, he was a Swiss physician, and the book was published in German. He was up at the front, and in German it is titled At The Balkan Front. It was published in 1914 and he medically treated the wounded Albanian soldiers in the Serbian military hospital in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 10 in the English, page 8 in the B/C/S. The foot of page 10, right at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page did you say of the Serbian text, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 8. The paragraph has been marked, and it's the end of the marked paragraph, and it says this: "Unlike their predecessors, the Partisans from the beginning made serious efforts to --" No, I'm going up the page a bit. "In 1944 to 1945 the Partisans put down major Albanian risings with particularly --"

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Ah, yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "... particularly intense fighting in the Drenica region." Now, I Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond want just to ask you a couple of questions about that. We touched the Drenica fighting or attack yesterday -- on Tuesday. We also examined a Cubrilovic document from 1937. You're aware, of course, that Cubrilovic also published an even more virulent memorandum in 1944, aren't you, for the Partisans?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. We'll come back --

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you think I'm mistaken, I'll give you an opportunity to look at the text a little later. At the foot of this page, it says: "Unlike their predecessors, the Partisans from the beginning made serious efforts to win over the Kosovar Albanian population, both by creating the Autonomous Region of Kosovo and Metohija within the new Republic of Serbia, and by taking steps to prevent many inter-war colonists from returning ..." Do you accept that Audrey Budding is correct in that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What assertion are you referring to? Because there are several here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The assertion that I've just read out, that they created the autonomous region and that they prevented inter-war colonists from returning. Is she correct in that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a fact, and I brought that up the other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 11. Page 8 in the B/C/S. Statistics.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Mr. President, might I be allowed to ask a question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, not usually. What is it you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have come here to testify on the basis of my report, and the topic that I have dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not allowing that. We will determine whether the questions are relevant or not relevant. We are here to protect you, and we will.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 11 in the English, page 8 in the B/C/S. And in the end, or towards the end of the paragraph marked, this sentence or couple of sentences: "Allowing for varying assumptions about the rate of natural population growth in this period, French social geographer Michael Roux believes that the approximate upper limit for the number of Serb and Montenegrin expellees is 36.000. (This figure is relatively close to the April 1944 calculation of a senior German official in Belgrade that 40.000 Serbs and Montenegrins had been expelled since 1941.)" The footnotes are given, and I think your estimate was a hundred thousand. Could you explain, please, why Audrey Budding is wrong, or do you accept that she may be right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot accept the fact that Audrey Budding is right. She just relies on Michel Roux, and I quoted dozens of different sources which arrive at a number of at least 100.000. And I also quoted the opinions of the British historian Stevan Pavlovic who says that the figures of the expelled Serbs range between 30 and 200.000. And he considers the top figure of 200.000 not to be realistic. However, he also considers that the figure of 100.000 is the most probable realistic figure, just as he considers that the number of Albanians who have come in and settled from 200 to 300.000 might be somewhat exaggerated. So the mean value is about 100.000 Albanians coming in to take up residence in Kosovo and Metohija. And I consider that this position by Ms. Budding is not founded on any primary and important historical sources. She does not say which German official she's referring to here, and I can tell you from other German sources that I have facts and figures that I quote in my report according to which, up until the spring of 1942, approximately 60.000 refugees found themselves at the borders of occupied Serbia, and I state that in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now let's move on - having identified where you're at issue with Audrey Budding on certain matters of fact, if they're important, the Judges will resolve them - to your page 16 and the English page 21. I'm having in mind, as I explained at the beginning, the thought processes or the belief system, seeing how it developed. We've already looked a little bit on Tuesday at the fall of Aleksandar Rankovic, and at the bottom of this page, your page 16, this or these sentences: "The parties post-Brioni attacks on police abuses and on centralism signalled the beginnings of a (temporary) democratisation of political life and a (permanent) decentralisation of the Yugoslavia party and state." Page 21 at the foot of that. I take it that you would, in general, agree with that, that there was a permanent decentralisation of the Yugoslav party and state?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot agree with that at all, and I have a complete opposing view to Ms. Budding, because I consider that the events that started in 1962 and 1963 and culminated in 1966 were the beginnings of the disintegration of the Yugoslav state. And I'm very sorry that Ms. Budding, who had previously written a very good doctoral thesis, sees a process of a state's disintegration which led to the disbanding of the state, and that she says this -- she calls this a process of democratisation. So my position is quite the opposite of Ms. Budding. I do apologise, but please allow me to finish. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to conclude?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, this impression that Ms. Budding has gained is not based on archival research, and I conducted research in the archives and reconstructed in detail when, in what way, and with what political goals in mind the process of decentralisation began or, rather, the destruction of the Yugoslav state, and ultimately this is what was borne out by the 1990s. The start of the country's decentralisation began in 1966.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we take away the word "democratisation" that upsets you, her description of decentralisation is one you accept, because --

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I apologise. No. No. Democratisation is something that is very close to my heart, and I am an advocate of democratisation of society and of states. But we're not dealing with the democratisation and decentralisation of a country here, we're talking about the victory of National Communist concept of Yugoslavia, which was catastrophic for the fate of that country.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We now read the next sentence: "The next five years were the most tumultuous in communist Yugoslavia's political history until the late '80s. Between 1967 and 1971, three sets of constitutional amendments were passed. Taken together, they inaugurated a new and far more decentralised constitutional order." Before I ask you to comment on that sentence, or those two sentences, and just for the sake of compactness, the constitutional amendments were passed between '67 and '71 and so the constitution had effectively been changed by '71. It was then formally set out in the '74 constitution, which is the constitution that people talk about and, so far as Serbs are concerned, complain about, but the amendments had been done in this four years. Do you agree with Audrey Budding's account that these were constitutional amendments that inaugurated a decentralised constitutional order?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes. They decentralised it but in the sense of destruction, of destructing the state. The manner in which the decentralisation was carried out led to the fact that the country couldn't function as a uniform state. Therefore, it was not able to function properly. I do apologise, but I have to complete what I've started to say. So this wasn't decentralisation in the usual customary political constitutional sense. It was a process of breaking down all the vital mechanisms of a state, and that is the essence of it. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not arguing for or against the constitution, I'm just trying to identify for the Court the landmark events established --

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 17 in the B/C/S, page 22 --

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the witness wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask you, Mr. President, to allow me to say a few words about this subject, because they're very serious subjects. I can't just give yes or no answers. I have to explain the position I'm taking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you're entitled to. Briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, the constitutional amendments of 1967 and completed in 1971, which later came to be compiled in the constitution of 1974, meant a definite end to the Yugoslav state. It put paid to the Yugoslav state. That federal state became a confederation, in fact, and Serbia was the sole area that was not a republic like the other republics. The provinces in Serbia were republic where Serbia was neither a republic nor a province and that was the absurdity of the constitutional position of Serbia within the frameworks of the Yugoslavia confederation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We go now to your page 17, our page 22. Observing in passing that one of the things that offended the Serbs was that in 1968, the name was changed from Kosovo-Metohija, Metohija being a Serb name, to Kosovo. And then we see at the end of this paragraph on the screen at the moment this sentence: "A province's borders could not be changed without the concurrence of the provincial Assembly. The provincial Assembly could make laws as opposed to issuing decrees based on federal or republican laws and the province would have its own Supreme Court." Now, Mr. Terzic, we're going to hear from other experts, including legal experts, and this is only part of the things that upset the Serbs, you will tell us, but is Ms. Budding correct in her emphasis that she places here on these aspects of the constitutional reforms?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if the Trial Chamber would truly understand the problem. We're not talking about an emotional understanding of the problem. This is a serious political constitutional definition of this problem. Kosovo originally means only the field of Kosovo, which is a small area. Kosovo and Metohija are two separate regions. They were always two separate regions. Mr. Nice, you proceed from the completely wrong premise that Kosovo is a separate historical or ethnic entity that Serbia incorporated. It's a different story. Kosovo and Metohija --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Terzic, the point I've made -- forgive me for interrupting you, but I'm aware of your desire to get away, and I'm just seeing if the report of Ms. Budding, in focusing first on the change of the name but then on this point of the changes in the constitution is properly reflecting some of the Serbs' concerns. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from that point of view, yes. She objectively -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go now to our page 29 in the English, page 22 in the B/C/S. This is a paragraph headed Albanians, and the first sentence really is all I want or -- no, the second sentence. We go back to 1956. As I said, I can't be entirely chronological in going through the report sequentially. "Rankovic's ouster followed by dramatic revelations of police abuses in the province led to fundamental changes in its government ..." Is it right, as Ms. Budding says, that there had indeed, before Rankovic's ouster, been abuses in the province against Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically that is not correct. There were repressive measures taken by the police, as Ms. Budding says in a different section, both towards the Albanians and towards the Serbs. But what Ms. Budding loses sight of here is a substantial matter, and that is that the security service discovered a ramified Albanian terrorist organisation with illegal weapons and so on. That is a substantial problem that she completely overlooked. Then you asked me about the provincial government, too. Yes. I want to say something, and I have brought some exhibits here and perhaps I can have them distributed to the Trial Chamber. From 1943 onwards -- no, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have your answer to the question --

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Albanians --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On this occasion, Mr. Nice will continue his questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Go now, please, to page 23 in your version, Mr. Terzic, and to page 30 in the English. Just again to try and get the sequence of events in our minds, the things that are important. And she sets out here that 1968 demonstrations. In a paragraph, she says: "The beginnings of reform appear to have fed rather than assuaged Albanian discontents. In November of 1968, violent demonstrations broke out among students in Pristina and spread to other Kosovo cities." She goes into that in some detail. 1968 is an event in the generation or creation of the belief system, isn't it, in Serbs? That's what I want you to confirm, because we don't have endless time, you see.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 1968 demonstrations are a significant part of the belief system. They feed into the belief system of Serbs about Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply don't understand this term that you've been using, "belief system." What does a belief system mean in your books? I don't understand it, you see. We are talking about historical facts. Of course I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and more simply. The 1968 demonstrations are thought to be important by Serbs as they addressed what they saw as the problem of Kosovo and Metohija, yes? That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only Serbs. I don't see why you are confronting only Serbs and Albanians here. This has to do with the fate of the Yugoslav state. Not only the Serbs but all of patriotic Yugoslavia believed that the demonstrations in 1968 were the first evidence of the Albanian separatist movement coming out into the open on the political scene. This jeopardised the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Serbia and Yugoslavia, because the slogans of the rioters were Kosovo to Albania, annexing Kosovo to Albania. So there was this slogan of a Greater Albania that was out in the open. This disturbed not only Serbia but all of the Yugoslav public.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what you told us earlier, but I must try and cut you short. We go now to - still with 1968 - to English page 32. Really at the very foot of 31 but let's go to 32, and in your text it will be on page 24, to record --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Could you please help me? Could you please allow me, as Presiding Judge, to say a few words about what Mr. Nice is asking me, and could you kindly ask him not to interrupt me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You will answer the question. And if you want to offer an explanation, you can offer an explanation. We are now dealing with page 32, and I have been, I think, fairly liberal in allowing you to offer explanations, because I appreciate that not all questions are amenable to a yes or no answer. Now, what's the question, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. And the Court will appreciate that although the report of this witness did not address Ms. Budding's report in terms that would make it easy to understand what was in issue, the exercise I'm going through is in part to establish more clearly what is in issue and what is accepted. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see on your page 24, our page 32, that there was a four-year period between 1968 and 1972 when some Liberals, notably Marko Nikezic and Latinka Perovic held power, and she suggests, does Ms. Budding, that they held power until Tito engineered their fall in October of 1972. She goes on to say: "During their time in office, the Liberals mounted a sustained effort to disentangle Serbia from Yugoslavia and Serbian from Yugoslav identity." Do you accept that analysis of that four-year period? And it's obviously summarised very much, but do you accept it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept that. I think that that is a very partial, one-sided analysis that is not based on historical facts. It is based on political assessments. The term "liberal" was given to them by Tito himself. You must understand the political system of Yugoslavia. In Tito's rhetoric, in the communist rhetoric, "liberal" meant something very pejorative. So this is a very one-sided assessment of this period on the part of Ms. Budding, in my opinion. And there's one more thing I want to say: The largest number of books in the Yugoslav society were banned during the time when the so-called Liberals were in power.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course Mrs. Perovic is still alive and active and writing and would hold totally different views from yours, wouldn't she?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mrs. Perovic very well. We worked together as colleagues. She's an historian now. We met many times. We talked. She took part in gatherings that I organised, but that does not mean that I cannot have a completely different view of that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only I. Not only I, but a large part of Yugoslav historiography.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, one thing that I've got to put to you, Mr. Terzic, is this: That there is indeed an existing body of intellectuals, including Mrs. Perovic, who would take a totally different view of the analysis of the last 50 years from that that you've given to this Court. You accept that, wouldn't you? There are intellectuals holding a totally different view from yours. It's not a unanimous view or anything like it.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. This is a hypothetical question. Quite simply I cannot assume what they would say. You will allow for the fact that all of us sitting here today will have completely different views of what is going on right now, so you will allow for the possibility of different people having different views. This is quite natural in the history of science as it is in all other sciences. There is no uniform view here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We move on to -- still in 1968, to page 34 in the English and page 26 in your text, to a paragraph that begins with the phrase "Among the figures ..." And then the third sentence says: "In a famous speech delivered at the Serbian Central Committee's 14th Plenum --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's trying --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. I beg your pardon. I've found it. Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "In a famous speech delivered at the Serbian Central Committee's 14th Plenum in May of 1968, Cosic, who had been a member of the committee since 1965, challenged the foundations of the party's national policy with an impassioned attack on Yugoslavia's growing decentralisation." Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And since Cosic may appear with subsequent witnesses as a person of importance in the developing ideas of Serbs, it's right, isn't it, that Cosic conceived, as early as 1968, the notion of partitioning of Kosovo between Serbia and Albania, or between Serbia and another state. He conceived the notion of partitioning.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any such thing, absolutely. In 1968, at the mentioned session, Cosic only pointed out that the question of autonomy and autonomous rights of the Albanian minority cannot be equated to the question of state sovereignty over one part of Serbia or Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. President, Your Honour. I really cannot give proper answers if this is the way these proceedings evolve. I need to say a few sentences because these are very important questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... say two or three sentences in explanation, then we move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in 1968, Mr. Cosic did not talk about any kind of division of Kosovo and Metohija at all. He pointed to the problem of national bureaucratism and the fact that the question of the rights of the Albanian minority is being projected as something different, and he says that there cannot be two sovereignties; there is either going to be Yugoslav sovereignty or Albanian sovereignty, and that is Mr. Cosic's position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you read Cosic's latest book?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some parts, not all of it. Not all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is he still maintaining that partition is a real, if not the only real, outcome that will work for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Are you advocating partition of Kosovo and Metohija or are you asking me what I think about Cosic's opinion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question is clear. He's asking you whether Cosic is still maintaining that partition is a real if not the only real outcome for Kosovo. You can either say yes or no or you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cosic, in 1968, did not mention any partition of Kosovo and Metohija. He mentions -- he has mentioned that question over the past few years. I absolutely disagree with such a position. Why would a part of the sovereign territory of Serbia be partitioned? Why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Mr. Nice was directing you to Cosic's latest book. Are you aware of his latest book? You said you had read some parts of it. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I even gave some evidence here, parts of that book. But if the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. If you have the question -- no, no. No, no. Listen to this, this is what Mr. Nice was asking you, on the basis that you have read some parts of the book: Do you agree or can you comment on the question whether, from that reading, Cosic is still maintaining that partition is a real, if not the only real, outcome that will work for Kosovo? What's your answer to that? It's a very specific question relating to your understanding of what Cosic was saying in his latest book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has to do with major political questions. You are asking me to take a stand with regard to a major political problem. I am telling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I think we have gone as far as we can with this. Move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I find this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I insist. I insist that I give an answer to this question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Terzic, the question is very simple. The question is what has been said in the most recent work. You must tell us as a matter of fact. It has nothing to do with your opinion. The question is a question a fact. Now, can you answer it or can you not answer it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which facts? Which facts does the question pertain to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Whether the author is now advocating partition as the only solution for the Kosovo problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not read the entire book, but I know from the newspapers that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your answer is you don't know. Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not my answer, that I don't know. I know of that position from what has become part of public opinion, but not a single state can reject part of its sovereignty. Why would Great Britain do something like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I want to move on with one more question about partition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're moving on. We're moving on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Time, Mr. Terzic, will not permit me to put the questions through you that I want to put because of the length of your answers, but I do want you to deal with this question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let Mr. Nice ask his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please listen to the question carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are not to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to lodge a protest, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Mr. Nice, ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If in due course the Chamber -- listen to the question. It's a hypothetical question which I'm allowed to ask you. If in due course the Chamber has a body of evidence showing that partition was considered by leading Serbs over the years since 1968, how does the willingness of leading Serbs to partition Kosovo fit with the suggestion raised by people, including the accused, that Kosovo is so central to the life of Serbia that it can never be let go?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, that's -- that's -- I'm not going to allow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a very difficult question to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope it's not difficult to follow. The proposition is, I think -- I may come back to it in another form, with Your Honour's leave, later, but can we then -- I'll pass over the letter from Tito, I'll pass over the blue book which is dealt with at our page 42, but they are important matters to which we will return with other witnesses, and references to the blue book at 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then we come to the next event of which you told us, which is the 1981 demonstrations of Albanians. But what you haven't told the Court about, Mr. Terzic, is the cockroaches. And would you now please explain to the Judges the importance of the cockroaches in the 1981 demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of the term "cockroaches" in relation to the demonstrations. Otherwise, of course, I know what a cockroach is. I wish you would explain the question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Are you saying you're completely unaware of a body of material going to show that the first demonstration at the university was apparently a student demonstration over the quality of food and famously over cockroach in soup? Yes or no. Are you not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that this is the first time I hear about these cockroaches, but I do know that as a pretext for the beginning of the demonstrations the quality of food was referred to, allegedly. However, if one looks at the entire context, it becomes clear that the illegal demonstrations, the preparation of the demonstrations, that all of this was just a pretext. I must admit this is the first time I hear of cockroaches. I know that allegedly it was the quality of food that was taken as a pretext --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have answered that. That's a sufficient comment on the question. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And are you aware of a body of material that suggests that the demonstrations that followed the initial student protest may have been generated by the intelligence services of Serbia or of other bodies and states in order to generate violence against which Serbs could react? Are you aware of a body of material that sets that out? Because you don't cover it at all in your report.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of it. I believe that these are mere speculations, because if one views the entire historical context, one can see the demonstrations of '71 and the demonstrations of '68 and the illegal organisations for years before that were preparing for this kind of thing, an uprising and demonstrations. So to claim that the Serbian secret service organised the demonstrations is something that is not serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you've never considered a book by Julie Mertus on how myths and truths started a war in Kosovo, a book that contains interviews with students? You've never considered that document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen the book, but I consider it to be a partial book, not an objective one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, this is the problem, Mr. Terzic, I must suggest for you: There is a body of material reported in various ways about the origins of the 1981 student demonstrations and raising the suggestion that they were stimulated in order to enable Serbs to act against them, and you haven't referred to it in your expert report. You haven't dealt with it at all.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm astonished, if I can put that way, with this lack of seriousness in interpreting what happened. The entire historical context of these events points to the contrary. This is something that is a pure invention. It has nothing to do with the actual evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask you -- may I ask you, Mr. Terzic, even if it is an invention, isn't it something that you would have commented on in your report as part of the history? Even if you were to dismiss it as being partial, why did you not refer to it, allude to it in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the history of science is something different from court proceedings. I took into account tens and thousands of very important historical sources that explain the process. I did not consider this assertion to be a relevant one because it was totally in contradiction to so many historical sources of primary importance. That is why I considered this to be irrelevant, because it does not explain the events that took place at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I hear your explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I should say, of course we don't have time, but I have the chapters I've referred to in that book available. I have the relevant extracts from Dobrica Cosic's book available, and I have material going to show the existence in Dobrica Cosic's mind of the partition concept in 1968 available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we turn to the last reference in Ms. Budding's report --

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in the English and page 37 in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Terzic, I'm not going to allow you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. We need to get on with this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 50 in the English, page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I put a question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no, no. That is abnormal. Witnesses don't ask questions. It's the other way around. Page 50?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 50.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question refers to where Dobrica Cosic mentioned the division of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am cutting you off because I have already allowed you to offer the explanation. You have offered it. I have heard Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond it. We have to get on with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page -- would you be good enough, please, Mr. Terzic, to go to page 37 in the B/C/S, page 50 in the English. And we see a reference here as follows: "The atmosphere after the demonstrations of 1981 proved just as hostile to reasoned discussion. In the early 1980s --"

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I cannot find it. Oh, okay. Okay. I have found it. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "By the early 1980s, they were pushing the boundaries of allowable action in a one-party system with mass petitions and marches on the Serbian and federal parliaments. The Serbian leadership reacted with hostility, but many prominent intellectuals embraced the Kosovo Serbs' grievances. To many Serbs in Belgrade and elsewhere, it became an article of faith that their co-nationals were being driven from their homes in Kosovo as part of a deliberate campaign of terror by Kosovo Albanians determined to create an 'ethnically pure' Kosovo. "The view was elaborated in a petition." Now, the petition is one of the untranslated documents that you've provided in your binders; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's wrong here because it says '68. It should state '86.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I think it does say '86 in the English, but still. Your petition, which I'm not going to deal with, alleged -- because you signed it, alleged and used the word "genocide," didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The word "genocide" is used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go over to 51 in the English, and I don't have time to go into this in any further detail, there is this paragraph where Ms. Budding says: "The petition is cited at length because it is representative of mid 1980s --"

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what page is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It will be either 30 -- a couple of paragraphs on, and it begins: "This petition is cited at length because it is representative of mid-1980s Serbian beliefs about the reasons for Slavic emigration from Kosovo. These were the grievances that set Serbian response to the Yugoslav crisis into a national pattern. It is therefore important to consider how far they were rooted in reality." And Ms. Budding says: "A full treatment of that subject would require a monograph in itself, and would need far more empirical data than has ever been collected." Do you agree with her that there is simply insufficient empirical data available at the time of the preparation of this report to decide one way or another on the facts underlying your petition?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I absolutely do not agree. It is regrettable that Ms. Budding is not informed. There were thousands and thousands of documents based on which these assertions are based. Thousands and thousands of documents. Also video records, audio records, correspondence. And I pointed to thousands of letters by Bishop Pavle. And there is a vast amount of documents on which these assertions are based. There was tremendous suffering on the part of these people, and this was clear. For me, it was not clear why Europe was being silent before the ethnic cleansing of one people by another people in the middle of Europe. In any other part of Europe, we would have had to react had these things taken place. This was happening in our own house, and Europe remained silent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... been identifying important events and matters in issue between you and Ms. Budding, and the Chamber can see her sources if it wishes to in the footnotes or end notes. I point to something entirely different. You were given the opportunity the last day to read in B/C/S a document prepared by the International Crisis Group on Pan-Albanianism. I trust the Chamber had an opportunity possibly to consider the document. I don't know whether it did. You know, do you not, that this document, the principal researcher for this document was Miranda Vickers, somebody you referred to yourself as a colleague; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the name of Miranda Vickers is not mentioned anywhere in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know that she works for the ICG and she was the principal author of this document, or the principal researcher?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that, and this whole document seems like a phantom document to me, because no single name is mentioned here of the persons who did the research. The only thing it says is the International Crisis Group spoke an Albanian journalist. The International Crisis Group spoke with such-and-such a person. They do not mention the first and last name of the person, where, and when this conversation took place, and so on. I assume that it was not Mr. Atasari or Wesley Clark who came to speak with these people. This document does not provide one single name as the author of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course you can go to the website and you'll find that her association with this is established. Please look at the executive summary. That's all I have probably time for, and one other passage. And if the executive --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I just have one request regarding Mr. Nice's question. I have a document which I would like to have copied and which I would like the Trial Chamber to see. Is this possible? This is in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's in relation to -- does it -- let us -- let us hear the questions that Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to the document of the International Crisis Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear the questions that are asked of you about the document, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the usher would be good enough, if we've got an English version, to lay it on the overhead projector. Page 1. The first page with text on it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, on the second paragraph: "It is instructive --" We can see: "It is instructive that both the KLA and the NLA started to gain popular support in Kosovo and Macedonia respectively at precisely the time when they moved away from their initial Pan-Albanian nationalist goals and concentrated on more rights for their own people. The Albanian national army, which overtly advocated a Greater Albania agenda, never managed to gain popular credibility." Next paragraph: "In Albania since the arrival of multi-party politics, poverty and international political conflict --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Internal political conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry: "... internal political conflict have eclipsed any aspirations towards expanding the state's boundaries. Albania is more interested in developing cultural and economic ties with Kosovo whilst maintaining separate statehood; and successive Albanian governments have opted for a strategic partnership with Macedonia." And then over the page and I'll ask you a question, please. Over the page, Usher, if you'll be so good. "In the long-term, Albanian nationalism will be tamed by full implementation of internationally-brokered agreements and respect for Albanians's place in Macedonian, Serbian and Montenegrin society, together with consistent pressure on Albanian extremists and politicians who appeal to them." And missing the next sentence. "Decentralising power in Macedonia and giving Kosovo conditional independence in return for an assurance that all Albanian entities in the Balkans, that the present borders of South-eastern Europe will remain unchanged, could also help stabilise the situation." Now, that's part of the summary. It's counter to the, if I may suggest to you, extreme position you advanced throughout your evidence-in-chief that this is the reality. Pan-Albanianism is a minority, not a majority position. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With sincere regret, I must state to the Trial Chamber in response to Mr. Nice's question that I feel that this document, the presentation of this document is a provocation. This document urges the establishment of Greater Albania. This is the platform of Greater Albania. The other name for it is Pan-Albanianism. Historians and linguists will tell you what Pan-Albanianism or Greater Albania means. We will look at another document, the Front -- The Albanian National Front for Unification denies this document and states that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just address this specific question that Mr. Nice put in summary of the passages that he quoted, and it is that Pan-Albanianism is a minority, not a majority position. Can you just give a brief answer to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely stand by the position that Pan-Albanianism is another name for Greater Albania. Number two, regarding independent Kosovo, the question of an independent Kosovo, or the question of the autonomy of Kosovo and Metohija was resolved by Resolution 1244. A clerk from this Tribunal, such as Mr. Nice, has no right to change Resolution 1244.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Terzic. Mr. Terzic, the specific question is that Pan-Albanianism is a minority, not a majority position. That's the specific question. Can you give a specific answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My position is that Pan-Albanianism has mass support amongst the Albanian people in Albania and that it is a projection of Greater Albania which radically threatens the stability of the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you attended and listened to the evidence of the witnesses Rugova, Veton Surroi, or Bakalli in this court? Have you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only partially that of Mr. Bakalli, and the testimony of Mr. Rugova, also just a part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you recognise that they deal in a very specific way with the options, the choices and what they wanted and what they want? And you recognise that it's contrary to their evidence that you've heard, even to the limited extent you've had, is contrary to your thesis, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, he has said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He only listened to it partially, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at two more passages of this report. Footnote 70, please, which I'm not sure of the page. It's page 17 in the English version, but it's -- if you could find footnote 70, Mr. Terzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Terzic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Chairman, I have a question. May I, in response to Mr. Nice's questions, provide a CD about the burnings of Serbian churches in Kosovo and Metohija, dated the 17th of March of this year? May I show this in response to the question by Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What question does this respond to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Terzic, we'll not allow it. It's not relevant to the question in terms of the period that we are considering.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Footnote 70, page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Terzic. Footnote 70. Aleksandar Rankovic was --

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which document? This document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the ICG document, your page 17, footnote 70, bottom of the page, please. "Aleksandar Rankovic was vice-president of Yugoslavia and regarded in some quarters as heir apparent to Tito. He headed the Yugoslav security police. The UDBA, as it was then known, was responsible for serious abuses of the Albanian population. On the pretext of suppressing Albanian irredentism, UDBA put pressure on Albanians to emigrate. Between 1954 and 1957, some 195.000 Albanians left Yugoslavia, and by the time of Rankovic's dismissal, the figure had reached 235.000." Now, you will have to discover later whether your colleague Vickers was involved in preparation of this work. Do you accept the accuracy of that footnote?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information in the footnote is not correct, and I offer an answer -- in answer to your question Exhibit 36 -- or tab 36 from my material, page 417, in which Jovo Sotra informs President Tito and all the leaderships of Yugoslavia and Serbia, and says that between 1953 and 1960, precisely the period that is mentioned here, only 16.000 Albanians moved out to Turkey. This is tab 36, page 417. This footnote that you refer to does not cite any sources. It's arbitrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My final question on this document, which you've had a chance to read, is that given the quite pronounced if not extreme position that you were arguing, speaking about in evidence, do you not accept that this recent document is a document you should have considered before coming to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not consider this document to be relevant in order to objectively present the events in Kosovo and Metohija. As far as I'm concerned, this document is the platform for Greater Albania and a platform for an independent Kosovo. It is an extremely political point of view of one group within international relations, and for me it's not a relevant historical source. It's a political opinion which is counter to Resolution 1244. I believe that it is an obstruction of the efforts of international community to achieve a high degree of autonomy of Kosovo and Metohija instead of independence, and this is provided under the Resolution. Urging or striving for independence of Kosovo would lead towards a very profound crisis in South-eastern Europe, so I believe this is a very dangerous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Since you seek to accuse this group of bias -- and I'm going to ask for the document in due course to be exhibited and considered by the Tribunal. Since you accuse it of bias -- please let me finish the question, Mr. Terzic. Would you explain what bias it is supposed to have. Is it part of an American conspiracy? Is it part of an Albanian conspiracy? We see the countries it works in and for which it has prepared reports. Tell us, please, where does its bias find its root?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the Presiding Judge would permit me, I would gladly do that. Number one: In the Crisis Group, we have Wesley Clark, who was the commander during the aggression on Yugoslavia. Morton Abramovitz is also part of the Crisis Group, who was an advisor of the Albanian terrorists at the Rambouillet negotiations. There are some other figures also which have not proved an objective stand in relation to all of these events. I will quote two positions from this document which clearly speak about the nature of the document itself. "An independent Kosovo --" This is on page 1: "An independent Kosovo is something that is quite different from Greater Albania. The plan by the international community is how to deal with the process of the final status of Kosovo without destabilising its neighbours in the process." Number two. This is on page two. I quote: "However, as far as the Albanians are concerned, this territory, meaning the territories in Kosovo, Macedonia, and Greece, for Albanians these territories are not separate, they are all Albania. They are all Albania, although divided amongst different political units with the borders from 1913, 1921, and with the later dissolution of Yugoslavia." I consider this text to be written by those political forces that wished to achieve an independent Kosovo and counter to the Resolution 1244, to take a part of Serbian territory out of Serbia. And I find that this is counter-productive. I find it to be a very dangerous step which would bring into question the stability of the whole of South-eastern Europe. Gentlemen, please. This entire document -- please, I would just like to say two words. This entire document does not mention a single --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have dealt with it sufficiently. You have dealt with it sufficiently. Mr. Nice, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is not a single word about Serbs or ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your report, Mr. Terzic, and your evidence is aimed at arguing the same position that the accused wants and is nothing like a balanced and fair representation of either history or the present realities. That's my suggestion to you. You've demonstrated that in every answer that you've given. You understand, you've come here to argue a cause, not to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not Mr. Nice's job to draw conclusions and judge about the testimony of the expert witness. That is not his job, and he's not qualified to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. That's -- that's a very ordinary question that is usually put at the end of a cross-examination, Mr. Milosevic. The witness will no doubt deny it and that's the end of it. It's for us to assess eventually. What do you say to the question that was put by Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Mr. Nice's question is not well-intentioned. I believe that it is not proper. I tried, on the basis of all available sources - foreign sources; British, German, French sources for the most part - to draw and present objectively the processes in Kosovo and Metohija, and with this presentation I wanted to help in the determination of truth about the fate in this part of the Balkans. I tried to be objective and to speak without any traces of rage or partiality, as they say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just please confirm --

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In irem estudia [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please confirm, when you got your appointment at the Historical Institute, you didn't have a Ph.D., I think, at the time. You'd only published one book; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I got the position at the Historical Institute, I was very young. I was 25 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were assisted in getting that position by influential people, such as Ekmecic, was it? Did he help you get the job?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Ekmecic lived in Sarajevo, and at the time I didn't know Professor Ekmecic at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it right that you --

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say -- I apologise. I must say that Academician Radovan Samardzic helped me, whom I recall with gratitude. Professor Ekmecic was a professor at the University of Sarajevo and at that time I didn't have any connections with him of that sort. And I regret that you are not well informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you also assist in a publication on the genealogy of Vojislav Seselj, even if you don't put it in your own bibliography?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. That's an intrigue. I can explain what it's all about, if necessary. The people's Assembly, the national Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, upon a proposal of the group of deputies of Mr. Vuk Draskovic, who is now the minister of foreign affairs, wanted to investigate the ethnic origin of Mr. Seselj, and that is something ridiculous. And they wanted us to provide our opinion on that. So the Historical Institute responded to that request and explained that the Historical Institute does not -- did not and will not be involved or work on the establishment of the ethnic origin of any person. Vojislav Seselj was not explicitly mentioned. We just said what there existed in documents on the origins of the Seselj clan, and that is all. So I regret that you are not very well-informed, and it would be good if you had more complete information at your disposal about the things you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the time taken by the witness in answering the comparatively simple questions, as I hope they were, on Ms. Budding's report means that I was not able to deploy the material I would like to have done. May the Pan-Albanian report become an exhibit because he has considered it and presents a contrary view available at the time of his report and we have heard his answers on why he says it's unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it may be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would have asked him to have dealt in detail with the chapter from the book on Kosovo, How Myths and Truths Started a War, dealing with the 1981 demonstrations which includes the interviews of students at the time and so is indeed both raw material and proper research, properly footnoted and so on, and I don't know if the Chamber would, in light of the way the evidence has been given, find it helpful to read that, because it constitutes a contrary view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The only other points that may be of value to the Chamber, they may be able to come in through other witnesses, are the witness denied the existence of the 1944 memorandum by Cubrilovic and denied knowing of Dobrica Cosic's earlier views on partition, all of which are covered by documents I can make available but, again because of lack of time, I wasn't able to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you have them, then you should make them available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I'll prepare that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Terzic, yes. Yes, Mr. Terzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the statement by the Albanian National Front for Unification to be adopted as an exhibit, about how they are in favour of an independent Albania, thereby going counter to the document by the International Crisis Group. I would like that to be tendered as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Terzic, the first document, the document that you wanted to have tendered, you say it is a response to the document that Mr. Nice just exhibited. What is it headed, and who is it from? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a memorandum of the Albanian National Front for Unification, of the 11th of April, 2004, and it's in direct response to a statement by the International Crisis Group. It's from the site of the Albanian National Unification Front, and I can provide it for you so you can make copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. We'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next tab number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if there is any clarification on who the National Albanian Unification Front is. If that would help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Terzic, tell us who is the National Albanian Front.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a very serious political organisation of Albanians which is striving for the unification of all Albanians and the creation of a Greater Albania within the ethnic borders as they consider them to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. We have admitted it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This memorandum will be D260.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Normally, it's the accused who would have documents tendered as exhibits. Exceptionally, we have admitted it. Mr. Milosevic, re-examination. Oh, it's time to adjourn. It's time to adjourn. We have passed the time. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before Mr. Milosevic commences with his re-examination, the Court Registrar would like to give the number again for the Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would like to give number 801 to the report dated 25th of February, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours also indicated that the material dealing with Cosic's position might be exhibited. I have that material available. I must identify what it is. There are three documents altogether. The first is a document from the Christian Science Monitor on the 17th of May, 1999. The second an a Central Europe Review of the 28th of June, 1999, dealing with Dobrica Cosic's earlier views on partitioning of Kosovo. And the third is the extract from his latest book, already available in both -- at least in this institution, in English and in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will admit the third, third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful. I'll make that available, and can it be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 802.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, lest you think we have forgotten your exhibits, let me say we will be dealing with them at the end of your re-examination. There are 51 documents that we have to consider. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Terzic, unlike Mr. Nice, I have to be highly economical with my time, so I'm just going to ask you a few additional questions, and please do your best to answer as briefly as possible. Mr. Nice commenced his cross-examination with the question of what was -- what did you have positive to say or write in your report about the Albanians. So my question to you first is this: Does your work, your report and other reports covering the subject matter of your own report clearly distinguish between the Albanian national community and Albanian extremists and terrorists, Nazi formations, terrorist formations towards the end of the century? Nazi, of course, in World War II and terrorists at the end of the century. So does it make a distinction between the members of the Albanian national community on the one hand and these other formations - extremists, terrorists, Nazis, and so on - on the other?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be very brief in my answer. From start to finish I always distinguished between the Albanian national minority, or ethnic minority, in Serbia and Yugoslavia and the illegal terrorist organisations and groups fighting against Serbia and Yugoslavia. So I made a clear distinction between the two and emphasised in several places that the Albanians were also the victims of those latter groups. So that exists in my report. I didn't make the division into Serbs and Albanians, but the Albanians who respected the laws of the country and those who did not respect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, your paper is entitled, Kosovo and Metohija in the 20th Century, The Political, Ideological, Demographic and Civilisational Coordinates of Ethnic Cleansing of Serbs from the Southern Reaches of Serbia. Therefore, it incorporates all those coordinates of the ethnic cleansing of Serbs from this area of Serbia. Now, you as an historian reviewing that topic, can you find a positive element in all this which you could attribute along with the conduct of these extremist, terrorist, or Nazi organisations? Can you find one?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke here about a phenomenon, and that was -- actually, I spoke about the history of Kosovo and Metohija in the 20th century. But within that topic one of the basic determinants that I mention is the problem of the ethnic cleansing of Serbs from Kosovo and Metohija. And I consider this not to be only the problem of the Yugoslav and Serbian society, I considered it to be the problem of European culture and European civilisation as a whole. Because if in any part of Europe a nation or ethnic group because of their ethnic affiliation or religious affiliation is being ethnically cleansed, that should sound the alarm for the whole of Europe. And I was only speaking about the violent expulsion and different forms of violent expulsion of Serbs from their lands in Kosovo and Metohija by the Albanian terrorist groups and individuals. That's what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Judging by your answer, then, I assume that the objection made is highly unfounded. The objection according to which you are approaching the matter in a subjective manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, well, that's not for you to comment on. That's a comment which is not warranted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Terzic, I hope you won't find it difficult, although it's difficult to find one's way in this pile of documents, but may we put on the overhead projector the English piece of evidence dating back to 1906. It is the English report of 1906 that we have in our documents, and could you place it on the ELMO. It's at the bottom of the page, as far as I remember, and it was underlined.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the title page of the book. This is the title page, and as far as I remember, that was the portion you're referring to is on page 89, if I'm not mistaken. 88, page 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Put that on the overhead projector, please, so we can see what it says.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you wish me to read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, may it be placed on the ELMO so I can read it too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Raise it up a bit, please, Mr. Usher. You've just covered the portion I'm interested in. And could we have it zoomed in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see here, it says Old Serbia and the Albanian border and then it goes on to say "[In English] Old Serbia is still an area -- Old Serbia is still an area of disturbances owing to the lawlessness and bitter and racial jealousies of the Albanians." [Interpreted] Yes, the racial hatred or, as it says here, jealousies of the Albanians. Now, do you consider this to lack balance this general position, because it doesn't say that the Serbs are responsible for that? It speaks about the racial hatred on the part of the Albanians and thus about chauvinism.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report, in several places, I quote an author called Mr. Brailsford in his book entitled Macedonia, and other authors who, at the end of the 19th century, speak about the racial hatred of Albanians towards the Slavs. And this was written by foreign authors, and there are a lot -- there is a lot of written material about that and I only used a portion of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to that, I'd like to draw your attention to another text offered to us by Mr. Nice. It is Audrey Budding's text. I don't have the time to go through the whole document in detail, but, for example, a quotation that he extracted from page 4 of the Serbian version of that text. And this is what he says. He quotes the beginning of the third paragraph on page 4, where it says: "Along with ever more frequent conflicts in Kosovo --" and this is what Budding writes -- "we see the first changes in the 20th century with the Balkan wars from the Ottoman hands it came under Serbian control. Modern observers in the Balkan wars registered normal a number of brutal instances on -- by Serbs and Montenegrins." That's what Budding writes. "Some people see that the soldiers took part in a systematic attempt to change the democratic balance of the area to justify its attachment into a Serbian state." Now, my question to you with respect to that quotation is can we speak about the inclusion or attachment into the Serb state of Kosovo and Metohija in the Balkan wars? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there was no change in status, because Kosovo didn't enjoy any special status in the Ottoman Empire. That's the first point. The second point is this: It was a question of the liberation of Old Serbia from Ottoman rule together with the other Balkan states; Montenegro, Bulgaria and Greece, countries in point. It was the first Balkan wars when the whole Balkan Peninsula was liberated and freed from Ottoman control. So it was -- that's what it referred to, the liberation of those countries from Ottoman control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, these regions, when and for how long were they a part of the Serbian state, these regions being freed from Ottoman rule in the Balkan wars?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs arrived in that territory in the 6th and 7th centuries. As a component part of the Serbian state, they had been there since the end of the 12th century. They were within the frameworks of a Serb state up until the end of the 15th century. From the 15th century onwards until 1912, in actual fact, they were under the Osmanli rule, Ottoman rule, but always foreign sources refer to these regions as parts of Serbia under Ottoman rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
