utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you a question with respect to the sentence I read out to you: "Modern observers in the Balkans wars registered the numerous bestialities perpetrated by Serb and Montenegrin soldiers." Full stop. That's where the sentence ends. And then at the end of that sentence or the beginning of the follow sentence, which goes on to explain what I quoted a moment ago, it says note 21, refer to note 21, and in note 21 or the footnote, whichever you like to call it, footnote 21 which you will find on page 3 of this attachment with the notes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note they do not have the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says the international commission to investigate -- and it is second part of footnote 21: "The International Commission to Investigate the Source of the Balkan Wars and Procedures in Them, Balkan Wars." It is Washington, the Carnegie Endowment, 1993. "For this assertion to be placed into the proper context, one must bear in mind the fact that the commission did not consider that the bestialities were conducted exclusively by the Serbs. It highlighted many bestialities perpetrated by Bulgarian and Greek soldiers as well and viewed that problem too as a regional problem," and only then does it go on to quote the passage from the Carnegie Foundation: "Those armed conflicts, open or covert, whether they were conceived in proper form always had the same goal, the complete annihilation of the alien foreign population." Now, what is stated in that footnote and the Carnegie Foundation, does it give a basis for Budding to say that Serbian and Montenegrin soldiers committed bestialities against the Albanian population systematically or was it the war effects in the Balkan wars in which Turkey took part on one side, Bulgaria, Greece, and Serbia, et cetera, this general conflict and war, was it the consequence of that? So from a historical viewpoint and from the viewpoint of wielding scientific apparatus, would that be a proper and correct assessment and observation to make by your colleague Mrs. Audrey Budding?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Carnegie Foundation shows this problem as a regional problem, as being a regional problem, but it was a large-scale war in fact between the Balkan Christians, all the Balkan Christians on the one side and the Ottoman Empire on the other. The war which finally liberated Europe from Ottoman rule. And in that war, just like in any other war, there were always crimes. Crimes were committed on all sides, and the Albanians took part in this war within the composition of regular Turkish troops, and irregular Turkish troops as well. So as I say, both sides committed crimes. But the problem was a regional one. However, the substance of the question, the crux of the matter, is something else. A report on the part of the Carnegie Foundation -- endowment cannot be the only valid source for what happened in this area. We have Russian, British, French sources, German sources of the day, archival material, archive sources of the day, and they are the number one sources, the primary sources testifying to this, of course, Turkish and Serbian as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to draw your attention to page 22, quoted by Mr. Nice, of the Budding report. The title is Albania, and then it says "The replacement of Rankovic was followed by dramatic --" I've been asked to read more slowly. I'll do my best. "The replacement of Rankovic was followed by a dramatic uncovery of abuse by the police in the province and led to fundamental changes in the provincial government, the most important being mass recruitment and promotion of cadres from the ranks of the Albanian majority." Now, to you as an historian, I'm sure you know the dramatic discoveries made of abuse by the police in the province after Rankovic's replacement, which Budding refers to in this all-embracing manner, generalised manner.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two problems there. First of all, my colleague Ms. Budding did not mention a single abuse. She did not specify. Second, in the reports by the organs from Kosovo and Metohija themselves, that is to say the Executive Council of Kosovo and Metohija and the Provincial Committee of Kosovo and Metohija, they spoke about certain types of abuses, but the main abuses were the amassment of weapons, for example, and the Prizren trial. In my opinion, all this was about the fact that the police had uncovered and prevented the activities of a large-scale Albanian organisation and, that was the key to the police's relationship towards the situation. But in the portion you read out, it said that it led to radical changes in the provincial government. Now, I have here a piece of information denying that position, that position taken. In a book published in Pristina itself, and I have here this piece of information, this document that I can hand round to all of you, it says Kosovo and Metohija in 1943, from 1943 to 1963, published in Pristina 1963, and there is a text written by Fadil Hoxha there. But I'm just going to look at some statistical data which refute Budding's position. It says: "A review of the composition of the regional National Liberation Movement, the provincial National Liberation Movement, and the Assembly of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija from 1943 to 1963," and here we have the statistic composition which shows that the Albanians, Albanian representatives were in all the organs of power and authority and they were the majority in those organs, they represented a majority. For example, the provincial national board from '43 to '45, the Siptars, as they were called, there were 44. Serbs and Montenegrins just 7. Now, the -- in 1945 to 1947, there were 110 Siptars and 41 Serbs and Montenegrins. The president or, rather, the Prime Minister was Fadil Hoxha. Mehmed Hoxha [phoen] the first time, then Fadil Hoxha, then the Prime Minister in '47, Fadil Hoxha once again. Deputies: Siptars 132, Serbs 66, Montenegrins, et cetera, et cetera. If we look at the period from 1951 to 1963, the Prime Minister once again Fadil Hoxha; the deputies, Siptars numbering 142, Serbs numbering 42. Then we look at the '53 to '58 period: The Prime Minister Fadil Hoxha; the number of Siptars was 46, the number of Serbs was 20. Then we go into the fifth composition of the government, '56 to '66 or '63, the Prime Minister of the Assembly, Pavle Jovicevic; the first Serbian Prime Minister, Fadil Hoxha; Siptars 54, Serbs 28, and so on and so forth. Until we come to 1963 where the president of the Assembly was a Serb, the Prime Minister was Ali Shukrija. There were 158 Siptars and 66 Serbs, which proves that in all the organs of power and authority, the Siptars enjoyed the absolute majority. And I can hand this round as evidence. I have sufficient copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think this is sufficient to draw the right conclusions, because this shows that Budding's report is quite arbitrary. Please, tell me now --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's not an appropriate comment. I hesitate but it's not an appropriate comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. All right. Is it appropriate to admit this report into evidence, Kosovo and Metohija, '43, '63, 1943, 1963?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's get the number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D261.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, please, Mr. Terzic, let us speak about the Drenica events and the parallels drawn to 1998. Budding says on page 8 of the Serbian version of her report, it's somewhere around mid-page, it will be easy for you to find it. Mr. Nice quoted some of it, and I'm only dealing with the passages that he quoted. "In the period from '44 to '45, the Partisans quelled large-scale rebellions of the Albanians, and there was fierce fighting particularly in the area of Drenica."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you said that the Partisans were actually already the Yugoslav army and that there were 30.000 soldiers deployed. So -- 39.000 soldiers deployed. So what you say and what she said matches in that respect. Here it says an Albanian uprising. Mr. Terzic, is this an uprising of the Albanians or is this fighting on the part of Ballista forces of Hitler's SS division in the area of Drenica in 1945 or, rather, a continuation of the war in the territory of Serbia, which was freeing itself from German occupation, that is to say Germans and Ballistas who were part of the German formations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Budding's methodology is very strange. She has Albanians on one side and Partisans on the other side. I must say that the commander of the Main Staff of the Partisan forces in Kosovo was an Albanian, Fadil Hoxha. After the military administration was introduced --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That will suffice, thank you. I wanted us to clarify this. We cannot simply make a distinction between Albanians and Partisans. These are Partisans that included Albanians, Montenegrins, Slovenians, Serbs, for the most part, of course, but also Croats and others. And on the other hand, the quisling formations, that is to say members of the regular troops of the Hitler coalition.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly, this is a struggle between the anti-fascist forces that included Albanians, and on the other side the Hitler coalition and its remnants from the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the word "uprising of the Albanians" cannot be used as appropriate there.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it can if it is a rebellion on the part of Nazi Albanian forces that rebelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's quite logical. So in 1998, again this was an armed terrorist activity in the territory of Drenica. You have information about that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So can you establish what -- what these two have in common, the Hitler coalition troops in 1945 and the terrorist groups in 1998 in Drenica.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What they have in common is resorting to violence in order to have a violent secession of a part of Serbia so that it could be annexed to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Terzic, for a moment I'm going to refer to your own report, page 109. You say at the end of the first paragraph that from January 1998 until the 10th of July, 1999, the Albanian terrorists in Kosovo and Metohija killed 1.835 persons. That is what you refer to in your own paper. This is correct, or it is just about accurate, because it turned out that they had killed even more people. Do you know that in that year, in 1998, the Albanian terrorists or, rather, the Albanian terrorist organisation that called itself the KLA, in 1998 killed more Albanians than Serbs? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. And this has been published too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in both cases, in 1945 and in 1998, it has to do with the fighting of armed formations against citizens and government; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if not absolutely leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, leading questions are not allowed. We've been through that before. You're putting in the mouth of the witness the evidence that you want him to give.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what's leading about the fact that I'm drawing a conclusion and I'm asking the witness to say something on the basis of what he said. That is to say whether both cases, namely 1945 and 1998, were clashes with armed formations that used weapons to attack the government and civilians, citizens. That is always illegal, although an effort is being made here to strike a balance between the legal organs of a state and a terrorist organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ask another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. This will do. This is sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Terzic, tell me, as an historian you have to rely -- as you said yourself, history is an interdisciplinary science, so you have to rely on demography, inter alia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the point of view of this science, is it possible to establish what is being attempted here, that the fact that Albanians were leaving Kosovo en masse and that that coincided with the demographic boom of the Albanians in the area? Is that possible from the point of view of science?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's not possible. This is an assertion that was made in the platform of the Albanian Academy Of Sciences, and it says, approximately, the more the Serbs expelled them, the more their numbers went up, which is an absurdity. The percentage of the Albanian population in Kosovo registered the largest increase registered anywhere in Europe in the post-Second World War period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You now presented this memorandum of this front.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the national unification of Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When you look at the website of that front, can you establish that they have their branches in Macedonia and in Montenegro and Greece; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can be seen on the memorandum itself, that they have such branches in Skopje, Pristina, Tirana and Ulcinj, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And in their memorandum they say that the International Crisis Group is lying when it says that it is not a majority position to espouse this Pan-Albanianism or this Greater Albania. And they give their own information and the results of their own research, so I would like to ask you for your comment. This is from the text that the Trial Chamber admitted into evidence. "Pro-national unification. [In English] [Previous translation continues]... per cent [Interpretation] 82.5 per cent. It is 82.5 per cent, [In English] against 6 per cent [Interpretation] Against [In English] 11 per cent. With what right ICG is ignoring that much more than 80 per cent of Albanians from all Albanian slants are pro-national unification." [Interpretation] This is self-explanatory, isn't it? So my question is whether this paper of the International Crisis Group is, in your opinion as an historian, of any scientific significance or is this merely a political document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, it is a political pamphlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you read who was on the board of the ICG?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I read that several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned Wesley Clark, who committed a series of war crimes in Yugoslavia. He's a member of that group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic, inappropriate. Inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the board, in addition to the persons you mentioned, is also George Soros. Have you seen his name?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen his name, inter alia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that this was a political pamphlet not a document that can be used for any scientific purposes unless people look at the substance of pamphlets in order to carry out scientific research.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If he says it's a political pamphlet and not a scientific document, let him say why. Why is that so, Mr. Terzic? Why do you say it's a political document and not of any scientific value?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, because its authors are anonymous. There is not a single name of any author who wrote this document. The only thing quoted in the text is the following: "The International Crisis Group interviewed or spoke to --" Who is the Crisis Group? The entire Crisis Group? That is impossible. That is one thing. Secondly, sources are unreliable. Sources are not documents. They are basically interviews with certain individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Isn't that the way documents of this kind are prepared? They don't always identify the authors. You have the board, the board members identified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is customary, Mr. President, for the author of the document to be identified. I don't know whether the members of the board are the authors of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. I take that point, yes. What are the other reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other reasons are very important too. This document advocates an independent Kosovo, and not a single word in it refers to ethnic cleansing of Serbs, crimes against Serbs. There is no reference whatsoever to Serbs in Kosovo and Metohija. This document is in contravention of Resolution 1244 adopted by the Security Council. That is one thing. It advocates the secession of part of a sovereign state, that is to say Kosovo, from Serbia. That is one thing. Secondly, it advocates a Greater Albania. Although it does not use the word Greater Albania, but it does speak about Pan-Albanianism, and under the term it means economic, cultural, transportation related, and every other kind of integration of all Albanian areas. What is that but a Greater Albania? If on the other hand one speaks of integration between the Serbs of -- from Republika Srpska and the Serbs from the Republic of Serbia, then this turns into the spectre of a Greater Serbia, so isn't that only logical?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Terzic, where did you work, say, in 1990 up to 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked at the Historical Institute of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the book by Ivan Stambolic which was admitted into evidence here, it is stated that some academicians at the time were toiling over maps. That's the word that was used, I believe. Please. You are in the same building. What is done at the academy is very transparent; everybody communicates with everybody else. Who were these academicians who were toiling over the maps in order to see how the Serbian lands can be linked up even along a goat path, as it was said?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any source.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He quotes a conversation with Vasa Cubrilovic; that's his source.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never present at any meeting nor did I ever see any meeting where these kind of maps was being looked into. Never, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you have no knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about this whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to take you back to this other very interesting issue that Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. There are research papers, there are scientific conferences that were public conferences. There were international meetings where maps were discussed, too, but from this point of view, from the point of view of building some kind of a Greater Serbia, I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assumed you would have to have information had such activities been carried out at the time.

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the director of the Historical Institute, I'm not a member of the academy. But I don't know about any activities of that kind in the academy in any shape or form.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go back to the infamous demonstrations. On page 23, Mr. Nice cited from that page, from the Budding report. I will quote just one or two sentences at the most. In the first passage on page 23, it states: "Some demonstrators demanded that Kosovo be given the status of a republic. That is the idea that the Albanians, including some officials, expressed earlier that year during the talks about forthcoming constitutional amendments. Some went even further, requesting that Kosovo and other regions in Yugoslavia populated by Albanians link up with Albania." Even Audrey Budding speaks about the demands for regions inhabited by Albanians be linked up with Albania, inhabited by Albanians in Yugoslavia. Now, could you please answer the following question: This unification with Albania of regions inhabited by Albanians be effected from -- as a result of finding cockroaches in the food?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any serious researcher is aware that we are talking about a long-term, well-conceived and well-planned project of several decades' duration, because these demonstrations are just an external expression of this project which was worked on by illegal organisations, which I spoke about, for decades. For this mention of cockroaches can be something that is humourous but it cannot be any kind of proof or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this reaction by students to the food they had in their dormitories, could that have been the cause of the events which ensued?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Pristina, you know, but if it was a problem with food, then you would be requesting better food. You would not be asking for unification with Albania, which at the time was much poorer than Kosovo and Metohija. This is logical in itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Terzic. It's logical to you, and perhaps to every other well-meaning person, but it's not clear to everybody. Could you please tell me, it was stated here that the Serbian service -- secret service incited these Albanian demonstrations in 1981. I am not asking you to say it did not, because this is something that everybody in Yugoslavia knows. What I'm asking you is the following: Are you aware that the Serbian service, as Mr. Nice calls it, had no access at all to the region of Kosovo and Metohija at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that and I regret the extent to which Mr. Nice is not well informed. Serbian services, Serbian police services had no jurisdiction at all in Kosovo and Metohija following the constitutional amendments in '68 and '71. Second, Serbia had no insight into Kosovo's international cooperation with Albania. So the conclusion can be seen based on that alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Terzic. Could you please tell us how the Yugoslav security service was organised up until the 1990s, until Yugoslavia existed. Was it centralised or was each republic independent in respect of these functions?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I'm not an expert on the security services, but knowing that all republics actually had -- were states within states, each republic had its own security service. I don't know what their mutual cooperation was, but I know that Kosovo had its own security service and that cooperation between Kosovo and Metohija and Serbia was not very strong in this respect. It was practically non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the security services and the police in Kosovo? Were they subordinated to the Serbian Ministry for Internal Affairs or to the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I don't know too much about it, as far as I know, and I'm not an expert in that matter, it was under the jurisdiction of the provincial Secretariat for Internal Affairs and probably under the jurisdiction of the federal security services, because I know there was a problem with the intervention of Serbian forces in Kosovo and Metohija. Serbian forces waited for several days in order to be able to enter Kosovo and Metohija in 1981. That is something that I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that then they only entered as part of the joint Yugoslav security forces and not as Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I think that the commander of that joint force was a Slovenian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that all measures adopted regarding Kosovo up until 1991 were Yugoslav measures, that Serbia practically did not adopt any measures about the imposition of any kind of measures in Kosovo and Metohija following the demonstrations in '68 and later, after '81, and all of -- and in light of all the subsequent events?

utterances.speaker: SLAVENKO TERZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's logical, because under the constitution, Serbia had no jurisdictions there based on the amendments and the constitution of 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Terzic. I have no more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Terzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, is it possible now to deal with the list of exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we're going to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I -- as I indicated before, I take it that if you have any questions to ask, you will bring that to our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic - and this of course will concern Mr. Nice - the Chamber overnight looked at the documents that Mr. Milosevic referred to in his examination-in-chief, and we prepared a list for ourselves for our internal use, and it numbered 51. The Chamber will issue an order as to the admission of these documents, and I will give a general outline as to the criteria which the Chamber will use. Those which have been translated will be admitted. Those which have not been translated will be marked for identification until they are translated. And those which have not been -- those which have not been dealt with will clearly not be admitted. And I should say that in relation to translation, it is only those sections that were referred to in court that will be translated. We can give a number to the binder now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D262 for two binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that give us the opportunity if we so decide, and I don't know that we will, to seek additional exhibiting of other passages from documents translated in part?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We think that that would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very grateful. And while I'm -- unless you had something further to announce by way of order, on the topic of exhibits, may I respectfully make one other proposal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Exhibits generally or in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. Exhibits generally and for this witness but not the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us release the witness first. Mr. Terzic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to give it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Terzic, are you in a position to leave the originals of the maps that were referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. I gave the maps to Ms. Evelyn and she scanned them in colour, and I trust that they are in her possession. But if this is not possible, I would be very happy to leave them for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Terzic. You may leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. The CD?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, maybe you can start.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the matter I wanted to raise is something upon which you've already ruled. It's the potential exhibit that covers the 1981 student demonstrations. You ruled against its admissibility and I'm effectively inviting you to give some reconsideration of that, for two reasons, really, but not -- first, it's been extensively re-examined on, including with such questions of the accused as "It's logical to you --" this was the witness's having answered something about the student demonstrations, and he said, "It's logical to you and perhaps to every other well-meaning person but it's not clear to everybody," and then he goes on to ask another tendentious question about the history of the 1981 demonstrations. The Court will recall that I'd explained that but for the time, and the taking of time was by no means entirely my cause, but for the taking of time I would have put to him an extract from a book, and I should explain that it -- although it's a book, it's an extract that is itself -- the chapter in the book is 30 pages and the footnotes run to a 160, is it, footnotes, so it's a researched document - 161 - and it's followed by some interviews, although, having said that, the amount of reading is pretty limited. And my concern is that if this is going to feature as an important part now of the accused's case and if there's no other witness to whom I'm able to put this particular piece of reading, the issue will only be fully ventilated if I seek and am allowed to call rebuttal evidence on a point like this, which of course one would be extremely reluctant to do given that, on one argument, it's at least historic and arguably peripheral. So my invitation to the Chamber is at any event to consider reviewing my application for that exhibit, perhaps marking it only for identification. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can you remind me of the title of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It comes from a book called Kosovo, How Myths and Truths Started a War. The chapter is headed The 1981 Student Demonstrations, and it reviews the various possible topics that I was able to raise but only very briefly with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who is the author of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's Julie Mertus. As I say, it's not just a book without authority, it's footnoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I raise something? Because it is important and I can't help but remark on it. We seem to be getting a lot of exhibits coming in from the Prosecutor which are unattributable that should be part of their rebuttal case if there is a rebuttal case. And vast tracts of evidence are coming in which are barely referred to, glanced upon, which can be later said to form some sort of foundation for their evidential propositions in this case. And it's of great concern that it may well unbalance the evidence in this trial. The accused, in my submission, is trying a technique that the Prosecution tried during their case, which was referring to a catalogue of tabs within an exhibit in a tangential way quite often and then seeking to have the whole of the documents admitted into evidence. We are getting into a dangerous area of trial by book and trial by chapters, unattributed people that -- the Trial Chamber has no idea the bona fides of these people, how they stand as witnesses, and we end up perhaps looking at secondary sources, tertiary sources, and not primary sources for evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, can I explain how I see this: The expert quite rightly quotes or identifies his sources. It would not be uncommon, following his evidence, to look at the parts of his sources he identifies. I for my part would not confine my reading to precisely the lines that were identified but I would look at it in context. And I hope that the order that we will issue and which Judge Robinson outlined will make it clear that that is the approach that the Chamber intends to take to the productions, to take them in context, have the bits that were referred to translated, not to admit the documents that weren't actually referred to by the witness. And I think that probably -- or I hope reassures you that we're conscious of the problem. And I think speaking for myself, I would be unhappy about admitting the document that Mr. Nice has just asked us to reconsider, certainly at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think the Trial Chamber, if a document isn't referred to, is entirely right in not admitting it. One of the problems for the accused in dealing with an expert on a historical basis such as this is vast sources have been looked at in the compilation of a report. And in the evidence-giving process, it is impossible within a trial to go through all the sources, all the references, but merely slide across them as they support his report, which, in our submission, the binders that were produced sought to do, to back up the propositions he had in his report. I appreciate the Trial Chamber is producing guidance which would be welcomed for all parties on it, but I do ask them to bear in mind the process that we had to experience during the Prosecution phase of the trial where we were admitting vast amounts of documents only at times tangentially referred to, but in the cause of the greater good because everyone was concerned for time and resources. And what we submit is that when the accused tries that process, that he should be given the same indulgence that the Prosecutor was. There's a danger now in looking at this second phase of the case that we forget the procedures that were adopted in the cause of economy and resources during the Prosecution phase of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. I think your remarks are timely, and we're always endeavouring to ensure that the accused is treated fairly. Mr. Nice, we'll not admit the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your next witness now, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My next witness is Cedomir Popov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may begin, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please give us your full name and surname.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: Cedomir Popov.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Popov, would you please briefly tell us the main points of your curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: I'm a university professor at the University of Novi Sad. I lectured on European history of the modern age, that is to say from the end of the 18th century to the mid-20th century. I retired after 40 years of having a university career, and I retired in the year 2000. In the meantime, I have gone through all the instances of university learning. In 1981, I was elected member of the Vojvodina Academy of Arts and Sciences. In 1981, I was elected as member of the Serbian Academy of Science -- 1989, I'm sorry. And when the two academies conjoined, the Serbian and Vojvodina Academy, I became a member of the Working Council of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences, of which I'm a regular full member. Throughout my life I have given priority to two aspects of work; that is to say tuition and scientific research. My books for the most part and the work I have written refer to the history of Europe and the Serb people within the frameworks of Europe, of European history, in fact. I was socially active by taking part in various cultural and scientific manifestations, scientific first of all in the province in the Republic of Serbia, and in the second Yugoslavia as well. I have nothing of particular interest to add, having said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Popov. And now something in your bibliography states that -- actually, we have a list of books published by you in the biographical extract. Not scientific works but books. And there are 13 books of yours published and four books which you edited written by individuals who dealt in areas of your expertise.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to tell you that the bibliographical notes and the curriculum vitae have been attached to Professor Popov's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Popov, which are the decisive factors, factors which had a decisive influence on the development of the national consciousness and awareness of the Serb people and the process of national integration? How did that evolve?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: There were two basic factors. One was a Balkan factor, a patriarchal factor, and an Orthodox factor in one - I would put that under number one - to which the Serb people belonged; and the second was the European component. So these two components came together and permeated each other, interacted in a fruitful way with each other during the 18th century at -- during the days of the rationalist philosophy and its supremacy and scientific thought in Europe. There was a meeting of the Balkan traditions which the Serbs brought with them to the Panonian valley with them, Podunavlje, which is the area of present day Vojvodina and Hungary, right up to Vienna and Trieste, and in today's Romania up until Terusvar, Arad, and so on. They stretched in these two areas. So these two traditions, these two cultural trends permeated each other and were very fruitful. They had a fruitful effect on each other. On the one hand we had the enlightenment, the baroque, the romantic movement which enriched the Balkan patriarchal culture on the one side and Orthodox traditions of St. Sava and the rallying of the Serbs which was brought from the Balkans during the period of the long resettlements that took place. They did not only take place in 1690, in the great movement under Arsenije Carnojevic but throughout the time of Turkish rule, that is to say from the 15th century onwards up until the end of the Second World War, and now, during current events after 1991, they were speeded up and multiplied even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Popov. Now, tell me, what was the relationship between the Serbian nationalist idea and similar ideas and ideologies and the policies waged by other European peoples, especially in neighbours of Serbia and surrounding Serbia?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: Serbian nationalist thought was very prompt in following what was happening in -- on the European scene in the broadest possible way, but particularly focusing on Central Europe, which is where we saw the development of a national ideology and social thinking based upon two key assumptions, premises, and they are the following: That they were all the members of one human group speaking one language, a single nation, a single language; and secondly, that this language, this common language, enabled them to have common -- a common cultural heritage and a joint endeavour to continue living in that fashion in the future. And the historical tradition here was very important in order to have the national consciousness of all these nations developed. And all the nations of the Balkans, Central and South-eastern Europe and even, if you will, Western Europe as well, enjoyed this process of enlightenment that the Serbs went through and formed their own nations on the basis of a common language, a common history, and common cultural traditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concept of Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're asked to repeat your question. The interpreters were asking you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the question wasn't interpreted and I'll repeat it. Let me repeat. I'd like to ask you to bear in mind that since we're both speaking the same language, Serbian, and everything has to be interpreted, what you and I say has to be interpreted, please make pauses between my questions and your answer to facilitate interpretation and avoid overlapping, and we'll save time in that way too. Now, my question was this: What does the concept of a Greater Serbia mean within the context of history and the national question in Europe of the 19th and 20th centuries?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: All the nations of Europe, including the neighbouring nations, nations neighbouring to the Serbs, had their national programmes with minimum requirements and maximum requirements, and they all had maximum requirements which transcended the requirements made by the Serbian national programme. A Greater Serbia is -- Greater Serbia is a concept which was introduced in usage very late in the second half of the 19th century. Up until then, the term used was "unification," first of all spiritual unity and cultural unity of the Serbian people; and after that, in the second half of the 19th century, we saw the birth of the concept of political unification of what was termed the Serb lands, that is to say the lands where the Serb people were in the majority. Neighbouring nations and nations belonging to other European countries who were also struggling for unification and for the creation of uniform national states, united national states, had similar programmes or identical programmes, but I have to say this, I have to make this proviso which might appear to be subjective on the Serb side: All those programmes were far more ambitious, if I might say so, far more expansionist and far more aggressive than the Serb national programme which limited itself exclusively to Serb lands or, rather, the lands and the area in which the Serbs were the majority population and in which they did not have any intentions of denationalising the members of other nations or other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Professor, what were the foundations upon which the accusations made against the Greater Serbia, what were they founded upon?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: They were usually founded on two ambitions: On the one hand you had the ambitions of the Central European powers, that is to say Austria, from 1867 Austro-Hungary, a dual monarchy that came into being; and on the other hand we had Germany, to permeate the Balkans, to break through into the Balkans, this is the Drang nach Osten which Germany designed after 1881 as an expansion, although these tendencies existed earlier on as well. But in this plan Austria or, rather, Austro-Hungary was supposed to play the role of the vanguard which was to open up the road to the German breakthrough to the east. That is one factor which led to the mystification of the question of the Serb nation and its aspirations to unite and to prevent this. The second aspiration which led to this was the aspiration on the part of the neighbouring nations to create their large states to the disadvantage of Serb territory, Hungary, Greater Croatia, which was under project from the middle of the 19th century, from Ante Starcevic onwards to the end of the 20th century with Franjo Tudjman. So these programmes were programmes that the Bulgarians had in their quest to take over Macedonia and the entire southern regions of Serbia, and even Greece too. The Greeks had these programmes too but they gave them up. They had them from the end of the 18th century and it was their great state and national programme which implied and envisaged the revival of the Byzantine Empire. So we see these two factors which collided or very often drew together in building up the myth about the fact that it was the Serbs who wanted a Greater Serbia to make it impossible for other nations to achieve their goals, and Austro-Hungary and Germany to implement their Imperialist plans to break through and reach the Mediterranean and Turkey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you be a little more precise and specific, please, and tell us who the creator of the charges against the Serb state and Serb nation was because of their alleged aspirations towards an aggressive policy in the creation of Greater Serbia and by subjugating other nations?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: This idea against Serb unity and unification appeared during the first Serbian uprising. This was a social and national revolution which corresponded very well to the revolutionary events that were taking place in Europe and the events that took place from 1779 to 1815. And it was from 1804, in fact, until 1813, to be continued in 1815, that we see this first stage of the Serbian national and social revolution which had a dual task; on the one hand to liquidate and destroy the Ottoman feudal system, which was very specific compared to the European social system but was identical to the Bourgeois European revolution, and on the other side to have the integration of the Serb people, which was the goal of Bourgeois revolutions in Europe. At that time, during that period, we saw the emergence of the great power, the big power factor, and they had their interests to promote in the Balkans and in the south-eastern reaches of Europe which were against this idea of the revival, renaissance of a Serbian state. We had Napoleon Bonaparte who, with his troops in 1806 reached Dalmatia, and he reached Bar and Ulcinj, and here he came up against the Turks. That was the border with the Turks. Then you had the Habsburg monarchy in Austria which did not wish to see a strong South Slav state on its southern borders. And ultimately, we Russia who, in material terms and diplomatic terms, helped the Serbian insurgents but did not agree to the creation of an independent Serbian state but, rather, was ready to assist it to gain autonomy over which it would have power and influence. So we have big power rivalry. And when this ended and when Serbia moved along the roads of building up its autonomy, for the first time in history we have Austria taking an express stand, or the Austrian monarchy and Metonic, who in 1816 already, that is to say after the first steps made in Serbia to create and reach autonomy, Metonic said that Austria did not see it as its interests in having a unified Serbia and a free Serbia along its southern borders. After that, we had the awakening of the interests of other European nations, and once Serbia gained autonomy nonetheless, in formal and official terms recognised in 1813, we saw that the big power -- in 1830 -- I apologise -- in 1830 we see that in this land had still not be sufficiently developed but they sent their consular officers and consuls and intelligence services, as did Britain, France, Russia and endeavoured to influence its policy and get a footing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milosevic, after that broad sweep, could we be a little more specific now. It's time to adjourn. It's time to adjourn, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it's on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before I put my next question to you, we have been dealing with the myth of a Greater Serbia, but I would like to ask you give me your comment. I'm going to read out from your paper, page 38, and you say as follows: "In order to eradicate this 'danger,' the Habsburg monarchy, before and after it was set up in 1867, dealt with every type of awareness of Serbian identity especially belonging to a national and cultural, denoted it all as a Greater Serbia or a Greater Serbian conspiracy."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You should identify the relevant page in the English text for us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a matter of fact, I haven't even got the text in English. I have to tell you that, Mr. Robinson. I thought that it was sufficient for me to look at the text in Serbian when speaking to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but we're following it in English. That should be part of your preparation, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Nice identified the text in English and in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can I get the text in English, because I haven't got it. I have it only in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Thirty-three.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If you found it, then I can quote it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "In order to eradicate this 'threat' before and after its reorganisation in 1867, the Habsburg monarchy labelled Greater Serbianism or even Greater Serbian conspiracy every aspect of expressing the awareness of the Serbian cultural and spiritual identity, particularly the awareness of the affiliation to a single national and cultural entity. A theoretician of Kalay's regime in Bosnia-Herzegovina described this in 1895 as follows: 'In essence, by its aspirations the Serbian spirit is nothing but cherishing the Greater Serbian idea on the basis of state and national unification of all Serbs.' "Accordingly, the Austro-Hungarian regime persecuted everything that could stir up the awareness of affiliation to the Serbian national unity throughout its Empire." Before I put a question to you, could you tell us, please, what kind of Kalay regime are we talking about? I assume that you mean Benjamin Kalay, but could you tell us briefly, what is the Kalay regime that you speak of?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: He was a member of the lesser nobility in Hungary and through the then influential Count Gyula Andrassy, he came into politics. In 1868, he was appointed to Belgrade as consul. He had learned Serbian very well before that. He even started writing about Serbian history, and in 1880, he was appointed Imperial Commissioner in Bosnia, and he remained there until his death, until 1903. This regime developed an idea that had already been in existence. It was not his own original idea, but it was widespread then, of this Greater Serbian danger in the Balkans and that this was a threat to Austro-Hungarian interests. If necessary, I can give you a few facts in order to show how this idea developed sometime from the middle of the 19th century.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: In the time of the Crimean war, from 1853 until 1856, the then foreign minister of Austria said that Serbia had to be eliminated or somehow put under firm control so it wouldn't spread its influence to neighbouring states, on the one hand, in order to prevent these states from becoming a Russian stronghold in the future. After that, the same idea but in more radical terms was expounded by Count Redburg [phoen] in 1862. He was the Austrian minister. So once in 1867 the Austro-Hungarian Empire was reorganised, the majority of the Serbs or, rather, the most active part of the Serbs remained either within Croatia or southern Hungary, and Vojvodina is part of it today. That is where many Serb cultural and spiritual initiatives were taken. The Matica Srpska, the oldest cultural institution, was there. Then the Serbian high school was there, the Serbian national theatre, and so on. The Hungarian authorities did not look upon this kindly. They even wanted to return Matica Srpska to Budapest in order to keep it under firmer control. Otherwise, it had been moved to Novi Sad, the centre of Serbdom. On the other hand, in Novi Sad a cultural, educational, and political organisation was established, that is -- that was called the United Serbian Youth. So this was a cultural society of ethnic Serbs from all parts of the Habsburg Empire, from Serbia, Montenegro, and Turkey. Various issues were debated there, cultural, ideological, literary, et cetera, but the Austria regime proclaimed that to be a Greater Serbian action and banned the organisation in 1871. From then onwards, and especially after Bosnia-Herzegovinian uprising in 1875, which was a major emancipation movement of the Serbs against the Turks in Bosnia-Herzegovina and certainly affected the attitude towards Turkey in Serbia and Montenegro too, the two Serbian principalities. And there was this large-scale campaign against Greater Serbian tendencies, and after the Berlin Congress, the Austro-Hungarian Empire was allowed to occupy Bosnia-Herzegovina and then ultimately to annex it, which indeed it did in 1867. So this campaign, speaking of fears from a Greater Serbia, was intensified all the time. And this went on, especially in times of crisis, in 1806, in 1811, and then in the period from 1908 until 1909, and then in the First World War the major struggle against a Greater Serbia was waged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you speak about this same page. Gentlemen, for your benefit, in English this is from the beginning of page 33, where it says the concept of Greater Serbia -- century. So this is what you say: "The concept of Greater Serbia was made public in the mid-19th century and was nurtured and further developed after the 1878 Berlin Congress, acquiring the character of a never-ending political and religious campaign. The aim of this campaign and the creation of the myth was threefold; to prevent the creation of a Serbian state within its national borders, to conceal the fact that Austria possessed some of the Serbian and Balkan territories and aspired to others, and to open the routes to a Catholic missionary campaign among the Orthodox population of South-eastern Europe. No effort was spared to spread the myth about a Greater Serbian threat, and they were constantly expanded. In the last decade of the 20th century, this myth promoted the small Greater Serbia to a threat for the national security of the only superpower in the world which was accepted and strongly supported by the German Imperialist Drang nach Osten policy, Klau fascism [phoen], Nazism, communism, and contemporary globalism.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the question on that? What's the question that arises from that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question is: Who participated in all of this and with what motives in the building of this historical myth of a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: Different big powers. Great Britain took part in the following way: It wanted to stop the expansion and strengthening of Serbia at all costs, fearful that it might become a Russian stronghold in the Balkans. It opposed this all the way until -- and then France, until its second Empire fell in 1870, also opposed this because they had different feelings about the Austro-Hungarian monarchy. And of course, the Austro-Hungarian monarchy opposed it for obvious reasons that were already mentioned there. And also the Catholic church was strongly opposed to this because, in terms of its missionary activities, it had built it into the idea of European national states through a few programmes and projects that were elaborated in Italy. Precisely at the time when Serbia was working on its national programme in 1844, Cesare Baldo wrote a book saying what Italy's hopes were, and he says the hopes of Italy are to have Italy united as a Catholic country, and also that Austria, as the proponent of the Catholic mission, should be sent to the Balkans in order to spread Catholicism there. In order to pursue such a policy, and promote such a concept, Cesare Baldo and all the other proponents of this policy enjoyed the full support of the Pope and clerical circles in Croatia and elsewhere, and both in the 19th and 20th centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. When answering one of the previous questions, you mentioned the first Serbian uprising, but you referred to it as the Serbian national and social revolution. My question is as follows, because this needs to be elaborated: What was the role played by this Serb national and social revolution from 1804 until 1815 in the history of the Serbian people in terms of laying the foundations of the Serbian national programme and in the national awakening of the Balkan peoples?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'd like the questions to be organised in such a way to facilitate short answers. The answers are far too long. So, Professor, we want shorter answers, and sometimes that can be achieved by the way question is framed. Yes. Please go ahead now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then I'm going to put three questions. What was the role played in the Serbian national revolution in 18 -- from 1804 until 1815? What was its role in the history of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: The heritage of bourgeois ideas which came through the Serbs in the Habsburg monarchy can actually be carried out. May I be allowed a comparison? The American revolution in the 1770s showed that the ideas of John Locke and other theoreticians can actually be carried out. In the same way, the Serbian revolution showed that the Balkans can espouse this heritage and carry through the main demands of the bourgeois revolutions. Perhaps I could repeat some of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is no need for you to repeat anything. That is the basic role. And what about laying the foundations of the Serbian national programme, this national awakening of the Balkan peoples?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: This role is also very important, because at the time of the first Serbian uprising, on Karadjordje's staff, Karadjordje was the leader of the first Serbian uprising, also in his Sovjet, his supreme council, there were two prelates of the Serbian church, Nikolaj Stratimirovic and Peter I, the Bishop of Montenegro. A programme of bringing together the Serb lands was elaborated. Karadjordje was very pleased with this and he tried to carry this through. So this was the first time that the unification of the Serbs was referred to, and it was the first time that there was this unification of the Serbian state. This is also important for other Balkan peoples, because the Serbian revolution gave a strong impetus to the movement in Greece, the Hetarus movement in Greece, Philike Hetairia, the Greek liberation organisation which was founded in 1815. And also a strong impetus was given to the liberation in Romania. Both movements actually came to the fore in 1821. So the Serbian movement gave an impetus to these other liberation initiatives of the peoples of the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not going to dwell on this much longer because it is in chapter 3 of your report. In the Serbian language it's on page 8, and in English it's on page 7, where it says that,"The Serbian people began its revolutionary transformation at the beginning of the 19th century at a time when Europe was vibrating from the powerful thunder of the bourgeois revolutions following the French revolution in 1789." And then you give these explanations that you've already referred to. Tell me, Professor, what about the national programmes of other European nations? What are their main characteristics at the same time, the first half of the 19th century when the Serbian national programme was being elaborated?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: If you wish, I can give you just a few pieces of information in terms of the German programme or the Hungarian programme or the Italian national programme, and so on. Hans Ulrich Weller, a German historian, analysed all these movements and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what are you seeking to demonstrate here? Is it that other countries in Europe also had programmes, similar programmes? I will consult my colleagues, but I'm not sure this is very relevant. Let us concentrate on Serbia. It's not really -- we are not in a university here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not academia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, this idea and this myth of a general Serb -- of a Greater Serbia is dealt with in a very simplified manner here. Academician Popov is highly competent to explain how these ideas were developed in the 19th century and what the historical context was in view of developments in other European countries at the time, in the neighbourhood of Serbia, in countries that were a bit further away, and so on. There is no need for me to prove historical facts. We have an historian here who is quite competent to explain all of this. But I think that everybody needs to understand the historical context in which this myth was developed, especially in view of the way in which this idea was abused here in this indictment. So that is why I believe this is relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must understand -- I must say that that was my understanding too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to be as brief as possible. Hans Ulrich Weller, you see, analysed three types of European movements for national unification where nations were created by the state. For example, France, Spain, the Scandinavian countries. Then where nations fought for their unification, like Italy, Germany, the Balkan countries. And finally, where they were created by seceding from big empires, and that pertains to the Balkan countries too. At the time when these ideas appeared, and when we refer to these three types, I have to tell you that this national ideology was the most highly developed in Germany, and of course I don't want to keep the Court much longer, but Weller quotes at least 11 German theoreticians. If you don't think it is necessary, I won't do this, but I just wish to say that this was not something that was specific to Serbia, the idea of a national state and national unification, and this creation of a strong country. That is what a great Serbia would mean, a strong country in which all the Serbs would live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you have identified the historical context in which the concept arose. Thanks very much, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Popov, what were the reactions by the major powers in Europe? Now I'm talking about the European major powers vis-a-vis these aspirations of the Serbs? In 1874 the rebellion began against the Turks.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that is the Serbian national and social revolution, from 1804 to 1815. What were the reaction of the major European powers?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: They were all negative. I think I said that a little earlier, and I can add to these facts that all the major powers responded to this idea of liberation and the independence of Serbia in a negative way right until the Berlin Congress when finally the Serbs, Montenegrins and Romanians were given the rights of a sovereign and independent state. These were all the guarantor states which protected the Christian peoples as far as they could within the composition of the Ottoman Empire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. We mentioned Garasanin's Nacertanije here. That is in the domain of your interest, the period, the historical period which is your speciality. Could you please answer the question of how Garasanin's plan came about? We had an expert witness report here provided by the other side, and he interpreted this plan, how it came about. So this is my question: How did Garasanin's plan come about?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: This expert work that you're talking about is the one by Ms. Audrey Budding which I came across by coincidence, and I think that that question was treated with a lot of -- with a lack of understanding. In fact, there is a definition there of Serbian national aspirations there, but Serbs were not those who initiated that. It came from Polish emigrants. Prince Milos spoke with a couple of diplomats, a British one, David Urquhart, and a French diplomat, Bois-le-Comte, and at about the same time in 1832. He expressed ideas to the effect that Serbs had aspirations to unite all of their lands into Serbia. Serbs not only in Serbia but also outside Serbia. David Urquhart brought this up before his government and published that in his magazine portfolio which he published, and besides that - and this is the most important - informed the head of the Polish immigration about that, Adam Chartoriski. When he studied this idea, it seemed to him that it would be a favourable thing to initiate in the Balkans with the assistance of the Serbs, a broad national movement aimed against Austria and Russia, because these two powers had divided Poland. And in the interest of liberating and freeing the Polish people, they felt that it would be good to initiate an action which would cause Russia and Austria to quarrel. He went on several missions. I don't want to mention names, but the decisive mission was one by Frantisek Zah, a Czech person who brought Chartoriski's instructions which the Serbian policy was to follow. He brought that in May in 1844. He submitted that to Ilija Garasanin, and then Ilija Garasanin worked that through. He edited it in the sense, because he left out Croatia from that plan, and he received a lot of criticism because of that for being anti-Yugoslav, because he divided a Serbian programme, but because of his own diplomatic caution in order not to irritate overly Austria, he also left out the anti-Russian leanings from that original instruction. So he formulated that in that way. I have it here. The programme was published many times, but it was held secretly in the safes of the Serbian government and the Serbian rulers until 1906, so for more than 60 years. The first time it was published was in 1906, and that is when the discussions began as well as contradictory assessments of that document which was assessed as a Greater Serbia in Serbian and a Yugoslav document today. I will not mention only Serbian historians, I will also mention an American historian who wrote a biography of Garasanin. This is assessed as a Serbian national programme, but that's the story of how it came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you rightly, Professor, the question that is being put quite frequently, whether the plan is Greater Serbia a Serbian or a Yugoslav programme, I understood your answer to be that it is actually a Serbian programme.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then why is it not a Greater Serbian document?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: It is not because it provided for the unification around Serbia only of those territories where the Serbian people are a majority, an absolute or a relative majority. And this -- besides the actual Serbia proper at the time, this would include Bosnia, which was Orthodox, where only Orthodox part of the population comprised 40 per cent of the population, but you also have Catholic and Serbs of other faiths. This is based on information at the time, because there was no real census in Bosnia at the time. All the way until World War I, Bosnia considered itself to be the most Serb-populated country of all the other countries. Besides that, there was also Old Serbia, the region of Raska, Sandzak, Kosovo and Metohija, because these were the -- this was the heritage of Serbian national history. On the other hand, at the time when the plan was being drafted, this supremacy of the Albanian or the Siptar population did not exist. The balance between the non-Albanian and Albanian population was disrupted only after 1878, when a very expansionist, and if you wish aggressive, Albanian national movement began to develop. That is why this document is not a Greater Serbian one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So that is the explanation why it is not a Greater Serbian document. You said which territories Garasanin considered to be Serb. What was his idea of this unification? How was it take place?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: It was supposed to be carried out in the following way: Without any revolutionary impact, without wars, by the gradual falling apart of the Turkish Empire, which was gradually falling apart during the previous two centuries, based on a particular type of law, not based on national and natural law. We would be taking those territories and unifying those territories which would break away from the Turkish Empire and in which the Serbian population constituted a majority. We would govern people from those countries who would be trained to conduct state functions and administrative functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, okay. So these were the views of Ilija Garasanin. In this concept, he speaks exclusively about territories where Serbs constitute a majority. Could you quite briefly, please, tell us in which way -- how did it come about that the Serbs came into possession of those territories which -- for which Garasanin said they were in a majority?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: Those territories were liberated by the Serbian state in the first and second Balkan war, and of course during World War I by uniting with them, with the exception of Macedonia, which was occupied militarily. So unifying with the other countries based on their own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Serbs from those territories expel anyone from those territories where they constituted a majority from the aspect of Garasanin's ideas?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: A part of the Albanian population in 1878 fled not before the Serb army but before the Serb people who had organised an uprising in Southern Serbia from Nis to Vranje. Nis is about 200 kilometres south of Belgrade, then we have Leskovac, then Vranje. The Serbian people staged an uprising there against the Turkish authorities, and the Turkish authorities were most directly helped by the Albanian population which was armed, the so-called Basibozluk. And then the Serbs began to retaliate. And this Serb retaliation prompted fear amongst the Albanian population, and they began to pull back. A large number of them went to Kosmet when the Serbian troops came, commanded by the first Serbian general, Jovan Belimarkovic. He stopped that immediately and even threatened that Serbian troops would withdraw if this pressure and terror against the Albanians did not stop who had been engaged on the side of Turkey. So this is the only case where we could say that Serbs, through pressure, removed a number of the population from the territories that they were liberating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what would the most frequent reasons for the condemnation of the plan as a Greater Serbian programme and Serbs were condemned as conquerors with pretensions for domination?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: This was all done based on Habsburg policies of Austro-Hungary in the most virulent form of the persecution of any kind of Serbian cultural or spiritual initiatives. There is a bizarre example for this: In Bosnia, sometime in 1906, thereabouts, the Serb Organisation of the Red Cross was banned because it had the name "Serb" in its name, Serb Organisation of the Red Cross. So you can imagine the fate of other Serb initiatives. On the other hand, the Austrian action met with the full support of greater Croatian ideas, because the Croats also had a fairly well developed national consciousness in the second half of the 19th century and it was much more expansionist and much more aggressive than the Serbian one, beginning from Ante Starcevic who negated the existence of Serbs completely. He felt them to be a branch of the Croats and he considered Nemanja and his state and his successors as Croats. So he negated the existence of Serbhood. And then on the other hand, Klaternik planned to expand from Salzburg all the way to Macedonia. Of course, it's understandable that such a policy and ideology which never ceased, it became a little bit more moderate since World War I, slightly more moderate, it stopped at the Drina River and the Sava and Danube Rivers, but that ideology was very anti-Serbian and it constantly attacked Serbia for Greater Serbia ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell me whether these accusations were founded, charging Serbia of ideas -- of desiring to conquer other peoples?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: Based on historical events and outcomes, today we can conclude or establish very simply and even assert that there were no grounds for such assertions. Here and there, there were incidents which were dramatised to a large degree and turned into historical evidence. They were mystified and so on. So the grounds for a policy of conquering non-Serb territories was groundless.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And these accusations were groundless also.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you please tell us if, and if so to what extent, did the Serbian national and political thinking of the 19th century was burdened with the Greater Serbian programme -- or not to say programme but plans; programmes and plans.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: The Serbian state programme and state policy, the official policy, never contained any Greater Serbia plans. It was always more oriented towards the preservation of what it had up until 1878, when its sovereignty was recognised. In Serbian society, there was some superficial or peripheral ideas about Greater Serbia. There was Pantelja, Milojevic and Sreckovic, historians who talked about the restoration of Dusan's Empire. The Serbian youth also entertained such ideas. But it was more of a feverishness rather than actual concrete plans.
