There was a magazine in 1888 which was launched by Ladislav Kacanski, a Vojvodina man who lived in Belgrade, which simply had to be closed down because nobody read it. There was no interest for literature like that. The only true movement for Greater Serbia stemmed from the annexation crisis in 1908, when the Serbian National Defence Organisation was formed, but after the crisis subsided, when the problem was resolved, this organisation turned into a cultural movement. But a group of officers came out of that organisation, about 500 of them, who created a secret organisation, Unification or Death, or the Black Hand as it was popularly called, and which advocated Greater Serbia ideas. They published a magazine, Piemont, which was an allusion to Piemont's movement in Italy. And at the time, the radicals were in power under Nikola Pasic in Serbia, and they managed to suppress that magazine in 1911. However, it was a little more difficult to suppress or break up the Black Hand, because 500 organised officers is not a small thing. And the Serbian regent Aleksandar and Nikola Pasic, the Prime Minister, managed to break up this organisation only during World War I, and the leader of this organisation, Dragutin Dimitrijevic, Apis, and two of his collaborators, paid with their lives for these subversive ideas, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is a very brief question about what you have just spoken about. What were the aspirations of the Serbian people in the 19th century?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: Always towards one thing; unification and equality with other peoples. If we're talking about Serbs from Croatia, nobody was thinking about including them in a Serbian state, but they themselves wanted equality. You know, in the entire political Serbian vocabulary during the 19th, the 20th, and even now the 21st century, the most often used word is equality, equality with other peoples, equality in sovereign functions of their state, in the exercise of such functions, cultural, spiritual equality, and so on. This aspiration was always the same: Freedom, independence. A free independent state and an equal position in those countries where Serbs were going to live outside of their homeland.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, in fact, that the Serbian people in the 19th century aspired to what it obtained at the Berlin Congress; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part, but understandably it was sensitive to the movements, and not only sensitive to the moods but it suffered a great pressure from Serbs in Bosnia and Southern Hungary or today's Vojvodina, in Montenegro; pressure from them, let's unite, let's become free and unite. And the Serb state avoided this because it knew of the -- it was aware of the troubles that that could lead to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, the Yugoslav state, the first Yugoslavia from 1918 until 1941 and also the second Yugoslavia, from 1945 to 1991, was it the sort of -- a sort of product of a Greater Serbian policy or was it founded upon some different foundations and interests?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: It was established and founded on the interests that I spoke about; to have all Serbs rallied in one state. But as that was not possible, in the Serbian state, the state of Serbia, and the aspirations became very intensive in the 20th century. They became very marked. And the prominent circles of Croatian politics, for example, and Serb politics in Croatia and public life -- the public life of Vojvodina province, generally speaking, and in other parts of the Habsburg monarchy, Serbia based its wartime programme, formulated in the so-called Nis declaration dating back to December 1914, said that its war objectives were defence, the defence of Serbia, and the liberation of the other South Slav brethren, because those brothers had asked for that. During the reign of the Serbo-Croatian coalition, for example, in Croatia, there were loud calls, although not always public ones, for this, because Austro-Hungary had some processes and trials. But there were numerous emigres, Croatian emigres, and so on in the countries of the entente exerting pressure on Serbia, saying liberate us, free us, unite us. And finally that programme was first of all set out by the Corfu declaration in 1917, it was put down on paper, and then later with the proclamation of the unification of all South Slav nations on the 1st of December, 1918. Now, there were different concepts within that project from which we see later on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Professor. Let's take it step-by-step, because this deserves a more profound explanation. You mentioned the 1914 Nis declaration, the Corfu declaration in 1917. Could you tell us what this was or, rather, were the wartime goals in the Nis declaration of Serbia, what were they? Were they Greater Serbia goals or Yugoslav goals, Yugoslav oriented goals? Tell us more about those documents, the Nis declaration, the Corfu declaration. Were they Greater Serbian in nature or were they Yugoslav in character?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: They were expressly Yugoslav war goals. The Nis declaration was formulated by the Serbian national Assembly, or Skupstina, of the Kingdom of Serbia of the day, whereas the Corfu declaration was signed by the representatives of the Serbian government and the representatives of the so-called Yugoslav board or council which was set up by the political emigres from the South Slav countries in Britain, France, and elsewhere, and in Switzerland in actual fact, in Italy as well. And they went along the lines of the unification of Yugoslav lands. So these two documents were expressly Yugoslav in character, a Yugoslav programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in this connection, with regard to what you have just been saying, we have amongst our exhibits several documents which speak about some important moments in the creation of Yugoslavia and the expression of basic ideas outside Serbia with respect to what was going on. For example, Frano Supilo's letter and correspondence with the British foreign minister, Sir Edward Grey, for example, and that is exhibit -- we have tendered that in the form of an exhibit. Could you explain to us first who this was, what this was all about. Who was Frano Supilo, and what ideas existed in his concept and what initiatives were taken?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: Frano Supilo was a prominent Croatian politician, a member of the Croatian-Serbian coalition set up in 1905. He was adverse to the Austro-Hungarian monarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where was it set up?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: It was set up by the Zadar and Rijeka resolution at two meetings held in 1905.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was a Serbian and Croatian coalition of Serbs and Croats living in Austro-Hungary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: Yes, in the Croatian banovina, or province, and in Slavonia and Dalmatia. Frano Supilo was one of the movers and creators of the Yugoslav board, or council, but in his political concept he included the idea of Ante Starcevic by which a Greater Croatia had to be established, which would incorporate and revolve around Croatia and Zagreb as its centre on the basis of Croatian historical rights, as they referred to it, and to create a Greater Croatia, which would encompass Croatia, Slavonia, Dalmatia, Slovenia, Bosnia, Srem, and the Bay of Kotor. And this would be one unit, one entity of a future Yugoslavia. The other entity would be made up of Serbia, Old Serbia and Macedonia, so that these two entities, these two units, would enter into a dual confederation similar to the one that was the Austro-Hungarian monarchy. The Serbian government and Serbian public opinion did not accept this for the very simple reason that that would, in a great Croatian state, would lead to an imbalance between the Serb and Croatian population to the detriment of the Serbs. The Croats would make up 38 per cent of the population, whereas in the Serb half, the Serbs would make up 70 per cent of the population. So outside the Serb lands, what you would have would be half the Serbs; All the Serbs from Bosnia, all the Serbs from Hungary or Vojvodina, today's Vojvodina, Slavonia, et cetera. And the Serbs could not agree to this kind of dual federation. What they wanted to agree to was a joint state in which they would all have national religious, cultural, spiritual rights, equal rights, and with their historical symbolism, that they would be on a footing of equality, the Serbs, the Croats, and the Slovenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about Frano Supilo's correspondence to Edward Grey or, rather, to the Yugoslav board?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, interpreter's correction: Letter to Nikola Pasic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this was a letter to Nikola Pasic presenting these ideas, and he distances himself from the other members of the Yugoslav board in that respect. The number one man, who was Ante Trumbic, he was a Dalmatian, a Dalmatian lawyer, in actual fact, and prominent politician, and it -- because he wanted to see Yugoslav on a centralist basis without this division into two entities, two units, the Croatian entity and the Serbian entity or unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the letter written by Stjepan Radic to the English government, British government?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: That was in 1922, once Yugoslavia had already been created. So Supilo was to be the starting point of a future Greater Croatian programme developed by Stjepan Radic in turn. He was, once again, a prominent politician, led the Croatian Republican Party and asked that within the frameworks of a united Yugoslavia there should be an independent and neutral, as he liked to call it, Croatia, a neutral Croatian state, in the Yugoslav monarchy, a Croatian republic. That was absurd, an absurd request, and it would incorporate all the territories mentioned, even more than proposed by Supilo, Backa, and Banat to boot. And that was a complete absurdity because that's where I come from. I come from those parts and I know it, I've lived through it, because you just have three villages who were -- who are in Romania now. They were just three Catholic villages, and by that token they were supposed to belong to Croatia. So these ideas were presented by Supilo in a lengthy interview to the daily news.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean Stjepan Radic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: Yes, Stjepan Radic in 1923, in an extensive interview which was to astound the Serbian public and I can say even a large portion of the Croatian public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we tendered that interview by Stjepan Radic.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: Yes, and it's very important for understanding this whole issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I think you're dealing with some documents which are included in tab 5, but I must say, speaking for myself, that that's not a proper way of dealing with exhibits. You have to deal with it specifically, each -- if you are going to tender it, you have to show it and put the question on that. General comment is not a proper way of dealing with the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Moreover, we don't have translations of those letters and interviews at all. And if I can say one thing more, that at least I would expect you to produce the index in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this index did exist and that several of the documents mentioned have been translated, because the Professor attaches a large number of exhibits to his report, but since they haven't been translated, I asked that seven points be translated at least, for you to be able to follow in English; and they are the letter of Frano Supilo to Sir Edward Grey, the letter of Supilo to Pasic, Stjepan Radic's letter to the English government, Radic's interview mentioned a moment ago by Professor Popov. It is the interview to the London Daily News, and later on to the Tribune. And King Aleksandar's 1928 map. I don't think that has to be translated. The Macek party programme and the Cvjetokovic-Macek agreement. I don't know whether any of that has been translated but I did truly believe that at least those seven points would have been translated. It's not such a big job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't have translations. I think very few are translated. Very few. But the point being made, Mr. Milosevic, is that in leading the witness in examination-in-chief, when you're referring to information that is in one of the documents, you must bring that to our attention. Otherwise, it comes across as a private dialogue between the witness and yourself, because we are not in a position to assess the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it you want to say, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I assume my word is some kind of evidence because you have 45 years of scientific research behind it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of course we respect that, but if he's referring to documents, then we need to see the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They can be translated, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, that is not your mistake. It is my mistake if the documents haven't been translated, because I expected that the portions we highlighted were going to be translated. And in tab 5, we have the book Yugoslav Federalism, Idea and Reality. Is it a collection of documents, in fact.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in that set of documents, that set of documents includes the documents that you highlight in your report that you mentioned a moment ago; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR POPOV
utterances.text: Yes, and ones that I attached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're now referring to tab 5, Yugoslav Federalism?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ideas and Reality. It is a selection of documents, or collection of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not translated. So we encounter the same problem that we had with the last witness. This requires a lot of patience, Mr. Milosevic, dealing with evidence of this kind. The strategy that we have been using is to have you identify a small portion, and we put it on the ELMO so that it can be translated for our benefit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're coming up to the time for the adjournment. It's a quarter to two. We're going to take the adjournment now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are adjourned until 9.00 a.m., Wednesday of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of December, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
